evidence_span.text: st_buffer(geography: geography, distance: float ) -> geography Returns a Geometry that represents all points whose distance is less than or equal to the given distance from the given Geometry. This function utilizes the GEOS module. This operation is done by transforming the object into a Geometry. This occurs by translating the Geography objects into Geometry objects before applying an LAEA, UTM or Web Mercator based projection based on the bounding boxes of the given Geography objects. When the result is calculated, the result is transformed back into a Geography with SRID 4326. Immutable

This function utilizes the GEOS module. This operation is done by transforming the object into a Geometry. This occurs by translating the Geography objects into Geometry objects before applying an LAEA, UTM or Web Mercator based projection based on the bounding boxes of the given Geography objects. When the result is calculated, the result is transformed back into a Geography with SRID 4326. Immutable

evidence_span.text: st_project(geography: geography, distance: float , azimuth: float ) -> geography Returns a point projected from a start point along a geodesic using a given distance and azimuth (bearing). This is known as the direct geodesic problem. The distance is given in meters. Negative values are supported. The azimuth (also known as heading or bearing) is given in radians. It is measured clockwise from true north (azimuth zero). East is azimuth π/2 (90 degrees); south is azimuth π (180 degrees); west is azimuth 3π/2 (270 degrees). Negative azimuth values and values greater than 2π (360 degrees) are supported. Immutable

evidence_span.text: pg_relation_size(relation_oid: oid) -> int Returns the on-disk size, in bytes, of the relation with the given OID. For a table-class relation this is the primary index size (matching PG’s “heap only” semantics, since CockroachDB’s primary index is the row data). For an index this is the size of just that index. The size is read from a periodically-refreshed cache and may lag behind the true value by minutes. Returns NULL if no such relation exists or has no on-disk representation. Volatile

evidence_span.text: TIMETZ , which converts TIME values with a specified time zone offset from UTC. Ordering for TIMETZ is done in terms of epoch . Time zones with lesser values are ranked higher if times are equal. For example, '2:00-1' > '2:00+0' and '12:00-1' > '1:00+0' . Like PostgreSQL , we implement the TIMETZ variant for . We also implement the TIMETZ variant for compatibility with ORMs, like .

evidence_span.text: CockroachDB supports precision levels from 0 (seconds) to 6 (microseconds) for TIME / TIMETZ values. Precision in time values specifies the number of fractional digits retained in the seconds field. For example, specifying a TIME value as TIME(3) truncates the time precision to milliseconds. By default, TIME / TIMETZ values have a precision of 6 (microseconds).

supporting_evidence.section_heading: TIME / TIMETZ

evidence_span.text: The TIME stores the time of day in UTC.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: TIME / TIMETZ

evidence_span.text: The TIMETZ data type stores a time of day with a time zone offset from UTC.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: TIME / TIMETZ

evidence_span.text: ​ Variants

supporting_evidence.section_heading: TIME / TIMETZ

evidence_span.text: TIME has two variants:

supporting_evidence.section_heading: TIME / TIMETZ / ​ Variants

evidence_span.text: TIME , which presents all TIME values in UTC.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: TIME / TIMETZ / ​ Variants

evidence_span.text: TIMETZ , which converts TIME values with a specified time zone offset from UTC. Ordering for TIMETZ is done in terms of epoch . Time zones with lesser values are ranked higher if times are equal. For example, '2:00-1' > '2:00+0' and '12:00-1' > '1:00+0' . Like PostgreSQL , we implement the TIMETZ variant for . We also implement the TIMETZ variant for compatibility with ORMs, like .

supporting_evidence.section_heading: TIME / TIMETZ / ​ Variants

evidence_span.text: You can use the and functions to convert a TIMETZ into a TIME at a specified timezone, or to convert a TIME into a TIMETZ at a specified timezone.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: TIME / TIMETZ / ​ Variants

evidence_span.text: We recommend always using TIME instead of TIMETZ . Convert UTC values to the appropriate time zone on the client side.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: TIME / TIMETZ / ​ Variants

supporting_evidence.section_heading: TIME / TIMETZ

supporting_evidence.section_heading: TIME / TIMETZ / ​ Aliases

evidence_span.text: ​ Syntax

supporting_evidence.section_heading: TIME / TIMETZ

evidence_span.text: ​ TIME

supporting_evidence.section_heading: TIME / TIMETZ / ​ Syntax

evidence_span.text: A constant value of type TIME can be expressed using an , or a string literal type TIME or type TIME . When it is unambiguous, a simple unannotated can also be automatically interpreted as type TIME .

supporting_evidence.section_heading: TIME / TIMETZ / ​ Syntax / ​ TIME

evidence_span.text: The string format for TIME is HH:MM:SS.SSSSSS . For example: TIME '05:40:00.000001' . The fractional portion is optional and is rounded to microseconds (i.e., six digits after the decimal) for compatibility with the PostgreSQL wire protocol .

supporting_evidence.section_heading: TIME / TIMETZ / ​ Syntax / ​ TIME

evidence_span.text: A date of 0000-01-01 is displayed for all TIME / TIMETZ values, but is not stored in the database. To print without a date, you can cast the type to a STRING .

supporting_evidence.section_heading: TIME / TIMETZ / ​ Syntax / ​ TIME

evidence_span.text: A time zone offset of +00:00 is also displayed for all TIME and values, but is not stored in the database.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: TIME / TIMETZ / ​ Syntax / ​ TIME

evidence_span.text: ​ TIMETZ

supporting_evidence.section_heading: TIME / TIMETZ / ​ Syntax

evidence_span.text: To express a TIMETZ value with a time zone offset from UTC, you can add an offset to a TIME value. For example, TIMETZ '10:10:10.555555-05:00' offsets from UTC by -5.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: TIME / TIMETZ / ​ Syntax / ​ TIMETZ

evidence_span.text: If no time zone is specified for a TIMETZ value, the timezone is used. For example, if you for a session using SET TIME ZONE -2 , and you define the TIMETZ as TIMETZ '10:10:10.55' , the value will be displayed with an offset of -2 from UTC.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: TIME / TIMETZ / ​ Syntax / ​ TIMETZ

evidence_span.text: TIMETZ is not affected by session-scoped offsets (unlike ). Time zone offsets only apply to values inserted after the offset has been set, and do not affect existing TIMETZ values, or TIMETZ values with a time zone offset specified.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: TIME / TIMETZ / ​ Syntax / ​ TIMETZ

evidence_span.text: ​ Size

supporting_evidence.section_heading: TIME / TIMETZ

evidence_span.text: A TIME column supports values up to 8 bytes in width, but the total storage size is likely to be larger due to CockroachDB metadata.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: TIME / TIMETZ / ​ Size

evidence_span.text: A TIMETZ column supports values up to 12 bytes in width, but the total storage size is likely to be larger due to CockroachDB metadata.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: TIME / TIMETZ / ​ Size

evidence_span.text: ​ Precision

supporting_evidence.section_heading: TIME / TIMETZ

evidence_span.text: CockroachDB supports precision levels from 0 (seconds) to 6 (microseconds) for TIME / TIMETZ values. Precision in time values specifies the number of fractional digits retained in the seconds field. For example, specifying a TIME value as TIME(3) truncates the time precision to milliseconds. By default, TIME / TIMETZ values have a precision of 6 (microseconds).

supporting_evidence.section_heading: TIME / TIMETZ / ​ Precision

evidence_span.text: You can use an statement to change the precision level of a TIME -typed column. If there is already a non-default precision level specified for the column, the precision level can only be changed to an equal or greater precision level. For an example, see Create a table with a TIME -typed column, with precision .

evidence_span.text: To limit the length of a string column, use STRING(n) , where n is the maximum number of Unicode code points (normally thought of as “characters”) allowed. This applies to all related types as well (e.g., to limit the length of a VARCHAR type, use VARCHAR(n) ). To reduce performance issues caused by storing very large string values in indexes, Cockroach Labs recommends setting length limits on string-typed columns.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: STRING

evidence_span.text: The STRING stores a string of Unicode characters.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: STRING

evidence_span.text: STRING is not a data type supported by PostgreSQL. For PostgreSQL compatibility, CockroachDB supports additional aliases and STRING -related types .

supporting_evidence.section_heading: STRING

evidence_span.text: ​ Aliases

supporting_evidence.section_heading: STRING

evidence_span.text: CockroachDB supports the following alias for STRING :

supporting_evidence.section_heading: STRING / ​ Aliases

evidence_span.text: TEXT

supporting_evidence.section_heading: STRING / ​ Aliases

evidence_span.text: ​ Related types

supporting_evidence.section_heading: STRING

evidence_span.text: For PostgreSQL compatibility, CockroachDB supports the following STRING -related types and their aliases:

supporting_evidence.section_heading: STRING / ​ Related types

evidence_span.text: VARCHAR (and alias CHARACTER VARYING )

supporting_evidence.section_heading: STRING / ​ Related types

evidence_span.text: CHAR (and alias CHARACTER )

supporting_evidence.section_heading: STRING / ​ Related types

evidence_span.text: NAME

supporting_evidence.section_heading: STRING / ​ Related types

evidence_span.text: These types are functionally identical to STRING .

supporting_evidence.section_heading: STRING / ​ Related types

evidence_span.text: Values of type NAME support subscript access with 0-based indexing. For example:

supporting_evidence.section_heading: STRING / ​ Related types

evidence_span.text: > SELECT ('hello'::name)[0];

supporting_evidence.section_heading: STRING / ​ Related types
STRING / ​ Related types

evidence_span.text: Out-of-bounds subscripts return NULL , matching PostgreSQL behavior.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: STRING / ​ Related types

evidence_span.text: CockroachDB also supports the single-byte "char" special character type. As in PostgreSQL, this special type is intended for internal use in , and has a storage size of 1 byte. CockroachDB truncates all values of type "char" to a single character.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: STRING / ​ Related types

evidence_span.text: ​ Length

supporting_evidence.section_heading: STRING

evidence_span.text: To limit the length of a string column, use STRING(n) , where n is the maximum number of Unicode code points (normally thought of as “characters”) allowed. This applies to all related types as well (e.g., to limit the length of a VARCHAR type, use VARCHAR(n) ). To reduce performance issues caused by storing very large string values in indexes, Cockroach Labs recommends setting length limits on string-typed columns.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: STRING / ​ Length

evidence_span.text: We strongly recommend adding size limits to all , which includes columns in .

supporting_evidence.section_heading: STRING / ​ Length

evidence_span.text: Values exceeding 1 MiB can lead to and cause significant performance degradation or even .

supporting_evidence.section_heading: STRING / ​ Length

evidence_span.text: To add a size limit using :

supporting_evidence.section_heading: STRING / ​ Length

evidence_span.text: CREATE TABLE name (first STRING(100), last STRING(100));

supporting_evidence.section_heading: STRING / ​ Length

evidence_span.text: To add a size limit using :

supporting_evidence.section_heading: STRING / ​ Length

evidence_span.text: ALTER TABLE name ALTER first TYPE STRING(99);

supporting_evidence.section_heading: STRING / ​ Length

evidence_span.text: When inserting a STRING value or a STRING -related-type value:

supporting_evidence.section_heading: STRING / ​ Length

evidence_span.text: If the value is cast with a length limit (e.g., CAST('hello world' AS STRING(5)) ), CockroachDB truncates to the limit. This applies to STRING(n) and all related types.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: STRING / ​ Length

evidence_span.text: If the value exceeds the column’s length limit, CockroachDB returns an error. This applies to STRING(n) and all related types.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: STRING / ​ Length

evidence_span.text: For STRING(n) and VARCHAR(n) / CHARACTER VARYING(n) types, if the value is under the column’s length limit, CockroachDB does not add space padding to the end of the value.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: STRING / ​ Length

evidence_span.text: ​ STRING vs. BYTES

supporting_evidence.section_heading: STRING / ​ Supported casting and conversion

evidence_span.text: While both STRING and BYTES can appear to have similar behavior in many situations, one should understand their nuance before casting one into the other.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: STRING / ​ Supported casting and conversion / ​ STRING vs. BYTES

evidence_span.text: STRING treats all of its data as characters, or more specifically, Unicode code points. BYTES treats all of its data as a byte string. This difference in implementation can lead to dramatically different behavior. For example, let’s take a complex Unicode character such as ☃ ( the snowman emoji ):

supporting_evidence.section_heading: STRING / ​ Supported casting and conversion / ​ STRING vs. BYTES

evidence_span.text: > SELECT length('☃'::string);

supporting_evidence.section_heading: STRING / ​ Supported casting and conversion / ​ STRING vs. BYTES
STRING / ​ Supported casting and conversion / ​ STRING vs. BYTES

evidence_span.text: > SELECT length('☃'::bytes);

supporting_evidence.section_heading: STRING / ​ Supported casting and conversion / ​ STRING vs. BYTES
STRING / ​ Supported casting and conversion / ​ STRING vs. BYTES

evidence_span.text: In this case, measures the number of Unicode code points present in the string, whereas measures the number of bytes required to store that value. Each character (or Unicode code point) can be encoded using multiple bytes, hence the difference in output between the two.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: STRING / ​ Supported casting and conversion / ​ STRING vs. BYTES

evidence_span.text: ​ Translate literals to STRING vs. BYTES

supporting_evidence.section_heading: STRING / ​ Supported casting and conversion / ​ STRING vs. BYTES

evidence_span.text: A literal entered through a SQL client will be translated into a different value based on the type:

supporting_evidence.section_heading: STRING / ​ Supported casting and conversion / ​ STRING vs. BYTES / ​ Translate literals to STRING vs. BYTES

evidence_span.text: BYTES gives a special meaning to the pair \x at the beginning, and translates the rest by substituting pairs of hexadecimal digits to a single byte. For example, \xff is equivalent to a single byte with the value of 255. For more information, see .

supporting_evidence.section_heading: STRING / ​ Supported casting and conversion / ​ STRING vs. BYTES / ​ Translate literals to STRING vs. BYTES

evidence_span.text: STRING does not give a special meaning to \x , so all characters are treated as distinct Unicode code points. For example, \xff is treated as a STRING with length 4 ( \ , x , f , and f ).

supporting_evidence.section_heading: STRING / ​ Supported casting and conversion / ​ STRING vs. BYTES / ​ Translate literals to STRING vs. BYTES

This may cause the result geometry to collapse to a lower dimension. supporting_evidence.section_heading: ARRAY

evidence_span.text: The ARRAY data type stores one-dimensional, 1-indexed, homogeneous arrays of any non-array .

supporting_evidence.section_heading: ARRAY

evidence_span.text: The ARRAY data type is useful for ensuring compatibility with ORMs and other tools. However, if such compatibility is not a concern, it’s more flexible to design your schema with normalized tables.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: ARRAY

evidence_span.text: CockroachDB supports indexing array columns with . This permits accelerating containment queries ( and ) and overlap queries ( ) on array columns by adding an index to them.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: ARRAY

evidence_span.text: CockroachDB does not support nested arrays.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: ARRAY

evidence_span.text: ​ Syntax

supporting_evidence.section_heading: ARRAY

evidence_span.text: A value of data type ARRAY can be expressed in the following ways:

supporting_evidence.section_heading: ARRAY / ​ Syntax

evidence_span.text: Appending square brackets ( [] ) to any non-array .

supporting_evidence.section_heading: ARRAY / ​ Syntax

evidence_span.text: Adding the term ARRAY to any non-array .

supporting_evidence.section_heading: ARRAY / ​ Syntax

evidence_span.text: ​ Size

supporting_evidence.section_heading: ARRAY

evidence_span.text: The size of an ARRAY value is variable, but it’s recommended to keep values under 1 MB to ensure performance. Above that threshold, and other considerations may cause significant performance degradation.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: ARRAY / ​ Size

supporting_evidence.section_heading: ARRAY / ​ Examples

supporting_evidence.section_heading: ARRAY / ​ Examples

evidence_span.text: You can use the && (overlaps) to select array columns by checking if another array overlaps the column array. Arrays overlap if they have any elements in common.

evidence_span.text: ​ Supported casting and conversion

supporting_evidence.section_heading: ARRAY

evidence_span.text: between ARRAY values is supported when the data types of the arrays support casting. For example, it is possible to cast from a BOOL array to an INT array but not from a BOOL array to a TIMESTAMP array:

supporting_evidence.section_heading: ARRAY / ​ Supported casting and conversion

evidence_span.text: > SELECT ARRAY[true,false,true]::INT[];

supporting_evidence.section_heading: ARRAY / ​ Supported casting and conversion
ARRAY / ​ Supported casting and conversion

evidence_span.text: > SELECT ARRAY[true,false,true]::TIMESTAMP[];

supporting_evidence.section_heading: ARRAY / ​ Supported casting and conversion

evidence_span.text: pq: invalid cast: bool[] -> TIMESTAMP[]

supporting_evidence.section_heading: ARRAY / ​ Supported casting and conversion

evidence_span.text: You can cast an array to a STRING value, for compatibility with PostgreSQL:

supporting_evidence.section_heading: ARRAY / ​ Supported casting and conversion

evidence_span.text: > SELECT ARRAY[1,NULL,3]::string;

supporting_evidence.section_heading: ARRAY / ​ Supported casting and conversion
ARRAY / ​ Supported casting and conversion

evidence_span.text: > SELECT ARRAY[(1,'a b'),(2,'c"d')]::string;

supporting_evidence.section_heading: ARRAY / ​ Supported casting and conversion
ARRAY / ​ Supported casting and conversion

evidence_span.text: ​ Implicit casting

supporting_evidence.section_heading: ARRAY / ​ Supported casting and conversion

evidence_span.text: CockroachDB supports implicit casting from string literals to arrays of all data types except the following:

supporting_evidence.section_heading: ARRAY / ​ Supported casting and conversion / ​ Implicit casting

evidence_span.text: Box2D

supporting_evidence.section_heading: ARRAY / ​ Supported casting and conversion / ​ Implicit casting

evidence_span.text: GEOGRAPHY

supporting_evidence.section_heading: ARRAY / ​ Supported casting and conversion / ​ Implicit casting

evidence_span.text: GEOMETRY

supporting_evidence.section_heading: ARRAY / ​ Supported casting and conversion / ​ Implicit casting

evidence_span.text: For example, if you create a table with a column of type INT[] :

supporting_evidence.section_heading: ARRAY / ​ Supported casting and conversion / ​ Implicit casting

evidence_span.text: > CREATE TABLE x (a UUID DEFAULT gen_random_uuid() PRIMARY KEY, b INT[]);

supporting_evidence.section_heading: ARRAY / ​ Supported casting and conversion / ​ Implicit casting

evidence_span.text: And then insert a string containing a comma-delimited set of integers contained in brackets:

supporting_evidence.section_heading: ARRAY / ​ Supported casting and conversion / ​ Implicit casting

evidence_span.text: > INSERT INTO x(b) VALUES ('{1,2,3}'), (ARRAY[4,5,6]);

supporting_evidence.section_heading: ARRAY / ​ Supported casting and conversion / ​ Implicit casting

evidence_span.text: CockroachDB implicitly casts the string literal as an INT[] :

supporting_evidence.section_heading: ARRAY / ​ Supported casting and conversion / ​ Implicit casting

evidence_span.text: > SELECT * FROM x;

supporting_evidence.section_heading: ARRAY / ​ Supported casting and conversion / ​ Implicit casting

evidence_span.text: st_dwithin(geography_a: geography, geography_b: geography, distance: float ) -> bool Returns true if any of geography_a is within distance meters of geography_b, inclusive. Uses a spheroid to perform the operation. When operating on a spheroid, this function will use the sphere to calculate the closest two points. The spheroid distance between these two points is calculated using GeographicLib. This follows observed PostGIS behavior. The calculations performed are have a precision of 1cm. This function utilizes the GeographicLib library for spheroid calculations. This function variant will attempt to utilize any available spatial index. Immutable

This function produces a 64-bit integer (i.e., ) from the current timestamp and ID of the node executing the or operation. This behavior is statistically likely to be globally unique except in extreme cases (see for more details).

evidence_span.text: The unique_rowid() function creates a unique integer composed of the current time at a 10-microsecond granularity and the instance-id . The instance-id is stored in the lower 15 bits of the returned value and the timestamp is stored in the upper 48 bits. The top-most bit is left empty so that negative values are not returned. The 48-bit timestamp field provides for 89 years of timestamps. CockroachDB uses a custom epoch (Jan 1, 2015) in order to utilize the entire timestamp range.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: SERIAL

evidence_span.text: The SERIAL pseudo is a keyword that can be used in lieu of a real data type when defining table columns. It is approximately equivalent to using an with a that generates different values every time it is evaluated. This default expression in turn ensures that inserts that do not specify this column will receive an automatically generated value instead of NULL .

supporting_evidence.section_heading: SERIAL

evidence_span.text: SERIAL is provided only for compatibility with PostgreSQL. New applications should use real data types and a suitable DEFAULT expression.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: SERIAL

evidence_span.text: In most cases, we recommend using the data type with the gen_random_uuid() function as the default value, which generates 128-bit values (larger than SERIAL ’s maximum of 64 bits) and more uniformly scatters them across all of a table’s underlying key-value ranges. UUIDs ensure more effectively that multiple nodes share the insert load when a UUID column is used in an index or primary key.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: SERIAL

evidence_span.text: The keyword SERIAL is recognized in CREATE TABLE and is automatically translated to a real data type and a during table creation. The result of this translation is then used internally by CockroachDB, and can be observed using .

supporting_evidence.section_heading: SERIAL / ​ Modes of operation

evidence_span.text: The chosen DEFAULT expression ensures that different values are automatically generated for the column during row insertion. These are not guaranteed to increase monotonically, see this section below for details.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: SERIAL / ​ Modes of operation

evidence_span.text: There are five possible translation modes for SERIAL :

supporting_evidence.section_heading: SERIAL / ​ Modes of operation

evidence_span.text: Mode Description rowid (default) SERIAL implies DEFAULT unique_rowid() . The real data type is always INT8 , regardless of the default_int_size or sql.defaults.default_int_size . unordered_rowid SERIAL implies DEFAULT unordered_unique_rowid() . The real data type is always INT8 , regardless of the default_int_size or sql.defaults.default_int_size . virtual_sequence SERIAL creates a virtual sequence and implies DEFAULT nextval(<seqname) .  The real data type is always INT8 , regardless of the default_int_size session variable or sql.defaults.default_int_size cluster setting. sql_sequence SERIAL creates a regular SQL sequence and implies DEFAULT nextval(<seqname) . The real data type depends on SERIAL variant. sql_sequence_cached SERIAL creates a regular SQL sequence and implies DEFAULT nextval(<seqname) , caching the results for reuse in the current session. The real data type depends on SERIAL variant. When the cache is empty, the underlying sequence will only be incremented once to populate the cache. When this mode is set, the sql.defaults.serial_sequences_cache_size controls the number of values to cache in a user’s session, with a default of 256.

evidence_span.text: The particular choice of DEFAULT expression when clients use the SERIAL keyword is subject to change in future versions of CockroachDB. Applications that wish to use unique_rowid() specifically must use the full explicit syntax INT DEFAULT unique_rowid() and avoid SERIAL altogether.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: SERIAL / ​ Modes of operation

evidence_span.text: Use instead of the sql.defaults.* . This allows you to set a default value for all users for any that applies during login, making the sql.defaults.* cluster settings redundant.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: SERIAL / ​ Modes of operation

evidence_span.text: ​ Generated values for modes rowid and virtual_sequence

supporting_evidence.section_heading: SERIAL / ​ Modes of operation

evidence_span.text: In both modes rowid and virtual_sequence , a value is automatically generated using the unique_rowid() function. The difference between rowid and virtual_sequence is that the latter setting also creates a virtual (pseudo) sequence in the database. However, in both cases the unique_rowid() function is ultimately used to generate new values. This function produces a 64-bit integer (i.e., ) from the current timestamp and ID of the node executing the or operation. This behavior is statistically likely to be globally unique except in extreme cases (see for more details).

supporting_evidence.section_heading: SERIAL / ​ Modes of operation / ​ Generated values for modes rowid and virtual_sequence

evidence_span.text: The unique_rowid() function creates a unique integer composed of the current time at a 10-microsecond granularity and the instance-id . The instance-id is stored in the lower 15 bits of the returned value and the timestamp is stored in the upper 48 bits. The top-most bit is left empty so that negative values are not returned. The 48-bit timestamp field provides for 89 years of timestamps. CockroachDB uses a custom epoch (Jan 1, 2015) in order to utilize the entire timestamp range.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: SERIAL / ​ Modes of operation / ​ Generated values for modes rowid and virtual_sequence

evidence_span.text: Also, because value generation using unique_rowid() does not require inter-node coordination, it is much faster than the other mode sql_sequence discussed below when multiple SQL clients are writing to the table from different nodes.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: SERIAL / ​ Modes of operation / ​ Generated values for modes rowid and virtual_sequence

evidence_span.text: Values generated by the unique_rowid() function do not respect the default_int_size or sql.defaults.default_int_size .

supporting_evidence.section_heading: SERIAL / ​ Modes of operation / ​ Generated values for modes rowid and virtual_sequence

evidence_span.text: Because SQL sequences persist the current sequence value in the database, inter-node coordination is required when multiple clients use the sequence concurrently via different nodes. This can cause and impact performance negatively.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: SERIAL / ​ Modes of operation / ​ Generated values for mode sql_sequence and sql_sequence_cached

evidence_span.text: Therefore, applications should consider using unique_rowid() or gen_random_uuid() as discussed in instead of sequences when possible.

evidence_span.text: Note that sql_sequence_cached will perform fewer distributed calls to increment sequences, resulting in better performance than sql_sequence . However, cached sequences may result in large gaps between serial sequence numbers if a session terminates before using all the values in its cache.

evidence_span.text: ​ Auto-incrementing is not always sequential

supporting_evidence.section_heading: SERIAL

evidence_span.text: It’s a common misconception that the auto-incrementing types in PostgreSQL and MySQL generate strictly sequential values. However, there can be gaps and the order is not completely guaranteed:

supporting_evidence.section_heading: SERIAL / ​ Auto-incrementing is not always sequential

evidence_span.text: Each insert increases the sequence by one, even when the insert is not committed. This means that auto-incrementing types may leave gaps in a sequence.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: SERIAL / ​ Auto-incrementing is not always sequential

evidence_span.text: Two concurrent transactions can commit in a different order than their use of sequences, and thus “observe” the values to decrease relative to each other. This effect is amplified by automatic transaction retries.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: SERIAL / ​ Auto-incrementing is not always sequential

evidence_span.text: These are fundamental properties of a transactional system with non-transactional sequences. PostgreSQL, MySQL, and CockroachDB do not increase sequences transactionally with other SQL statements, so these effects can happen in any case.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: SERIAL / ​ Auto-incrementing is not always sequential

evidence_span.text: To experience this for yourself, run through the following example in PostgreSQL:

supporting_evidence.section_heading: SERIAL / ​ Auto-incrementing is not always sequential

evidence_span.text: Create a table with a SERIAL column:

supporting_evidence.section_heading: SERIAL / ​ Auto-incrementing is not always sequential

evidence_span.text: > CREATE TABLE increment (a SERIAL PRIMARY KEY);

supporting_evidence.section_heading: SERIAL / ​ Auto-incrementing is not always sequential

evidence_span.text: Run four transactions for inserting rows:

supporting_evidence.section_heading: SERIAL / ​ Auto-incrementing is not always sequential
SERIAL / ​ Auto-incrementing is not always sequential
SERIAL / ​ Auto-incrementing is not always sequential
SERIAL / ​ Auto-incrementing is not always sequential
SERIAL / ​ Auto-incrementing is not always sequential

evidence_span.text: View the rows created:

supporting_evidence.section_heading: SERIAL / ​ Auto-incrementing is not always sequential

evidence_span.text: > SELECT * from increment;

supporting_evidence.section_heading: SERIAL / ​ Auto-incrementing is not always sequential
SERIAL / ​ Auto-incrementing is not always sequential

evidence_span.text: Since each insert increased the sequence in column a by one, the first committed insert got the value 645994218934534145 , and the second committed insert got the value 645994218978082817 . As you can see, the values aren’t strictly sequential, and the last value doesn’t give an accurate count of rows in the table.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: SERIAL / ​ Auto-incrementing is not always sequential

evidence_span.text: In summary, the SERIAL type in PostgreSQL and CockroachDB, and the AUTO_INCREMENT type in MySQL, all behave the same in that they do not create strict sequences. CockroachDB will likely create more gaps than these other databases, but will generate these values much faster. An alternative is to use .

supporting_evidence.section_heading: SERIAL / ​ Auto-incrementing is not always sequential

evidence_span.text: ​ Additional scenarios

supporting_evidence.section_heading: SERIAL / ​ Auto-incrementing is not always sequential

evidence_span.text: If two transactions occur concurrently, CockroachDB cannot guarantee monotonically increasing IDs (i.e., first commit is smaller than second commit). Here are three more scenarios that demonstrate this:

supporting_evidence.section_heading: SERIAL / ​ Auto-incrementing is not always sequential / ​ Additional scenarios

evidence_span.text: ​ Scenario 1

supporting_evidence.section_heading: SERIAL / ​ Auto-incrementing is not always sequential / ​ Additional scenarios

evidence_span.text: At time 1, transaction T1 BEGIN s.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: SERIAL / ​ Auto-incrementing is not always sequential / ​ Additional scenarios / ​ Scenario 1

evidence_span.text: At time 2, transaction T2 BEGIN s on the same node (from a different client).

supporting_evidence.section_heading: SERIAL / ​ Auto-incrementing is not always sequential / ​ Additional scenarios / ​ Scenario 1

evidence_span.text: At time 3, transaction T1 creates a SERIAL value, x .

supporting_evidence.section_heading: SERIAL / ​ Auto-incrementing is not always sequential / ​ Additional scenarios / ​ Scenario 1

evidence_span.text: At time 3 + 2 microseconds, transaction T2 creates a SERIAL value, y .

supporting_evidence.section_heading: SERIAL / ​ Auto-incrementing is not always sequential / ​ Additional scenarios / ​ Scenario 1

evidence_span.text: At time 4, transaction T1 COMMIT s.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: SERIAL / ​ Auto-incrementing is not always sequential / ​ Additional scenarios / ​ Scenario 1

evidence_span.text: At time 5, transaction T2 COMMIT s.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: SERIAL / ​ Auto-incrementing is not always sequential / ​ Additional scenarios / ​ Scenario 1

evidence_span.text: If this happens, CockroachDB cannot guarantee whether x < y or x > y , despite the fact T1 and T2 began and were committed in different times. In this particular example, it’s even likely that x = y because there is less than a 10-microsecond difference and the SERIAL values are constructed from the number of microseconds in the current time.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: SERIAL / ​ Auto-incrementing is not always sequential / ​ Additional scenarios / ​ Scenario 1

evidence_span.text: ​ Scenario 2

supporting_evidence.section_heading: SERIAL / ​ Auto-incrementing is not always sequential / ​ Additional scenarios

evidence_span.text: At time 1, transaction T1 BEGIN s.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: SERIAL / ​ Auto-incrementing is not always sequential / ​ Additional scenarios / ​ Scenario 2

evidence_span.text: At time 1, transaction T2 BEGIN s somewhere else, on a different node.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: SERIAL / ​ Auto-incrementing is not always sequential / ​ Additional scenarios / ​ Scenario 2

evidence_span.text: At time 2, transaction T1 creates a SERIAL value, x .

supporting_evidence.section_heading: SERIAL / ​ Auto-incrementing is not always sequential / ​ Additional scenarios / ​ Scenario 2

evidence_span.text: At time 3, transaction T2 creates a SERIAL value, y .

supporting_evidence.section_heading: SERIAL / ​ Auto-incrementing is not always sequential / ​ Additional scenarios / ​ Scenario 2

evidence_span.text: At time 4, transaction T1 COMMIT s.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: SERIAL / ​ Auto-incrementing is not always sequential / ​ Additional scenarios / ​ Scenario 2

evidence_span.text: At time 4, transaction T2 COMMIT s.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: SERIAL / ​ Auto-incrementing is not always sequential / ​ Additional scenarios / ​ Scenario 2

evidence_span.text: If this happens, CockroachDB cannot guarantee whether x < y or x > y . Both can happen, even though the transactions began and committed at the same time. However it’s sure that x != y because the values were generated on different nodes.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: SERIAL / ​ Auto-incrementing is not always sequential / ​ Additional scenarios / ​ Scenario 2

evidence_span.text: ​ Scenario 3

supporting_evidence.section_heading: SERIAL / ​ Auto-incrementing is not always sequential / ​ Additional scenarios

evidence_span.text: At time 1, transaction T1 BEGIN s.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: SERIAL / ​ Auto-incrementing is not always sequential / ​ Additional scenarios / ​ Scenario 3

evidence_span.text: At time 2, transaction T1 creates a SERIAL value, x .

supporting_evidence.section_heading: SERIAL / ​ Auto-incrementing is not always sequential / ​ Additional scenarios / ​ Scenario 3

evidence_span.text: At time 3, transaction T1 COMMIT s.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: SERIAL / ​ Auto-incrementing is not always sequential / ​ Additional scenarios / ​ Scenario 3

evidence_span.text: At time 4, transaction T2 BEGIN s somewhere else, on a different node.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: SERIAL / ​ Auto-incrementing is not always sequential / ​ Additional scenarios / ​ Scenario 3

evidence_span.text: At time 5, transaction T2 creates a SERIAL value, y .

supporting_evidence.section_heading: SERIAL / ​ Auto-incrementing is not always sequential / ​ Additional scenarios / ​ Scenario 3

evidence_span.text: At time 6, transaction T2 COMMIT s.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: SERIAL / ​ Auto-incrementing is not always sequential / ​ Additional scenarios / ​ Scenario 3

evidence_span.text: There is less than a 250-microsecond difference between the system clocks of the two nodes.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: SERIAL / ​ Auto-incrementing is not always sequential / ​ Additional scenarios / ​ Scenario 3

evidence_span.text: If this happens, CockroachDB cannot guarantee whether x < y or x > y . Even though the transactions “clearly” occurred one “after” the other, perhaps there was a clock skew between the two nodes and the system time of the second node is set earlier than the first node.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: SERIAL / ​ Auto-incrementing is not always sequential / ​ Additional scenarios / ​ Scenario 3

evidence_span.text: ​ Use SERIAL to auto-generate primary keys

supporting_evidence.section_heading: SERIAL / ​ Example

evidence_span.text: In this example, we create a table with the SERIAL column as the primary key so we can auto-generate unique IDs on insert.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: SERIAL / ​ Example / ​ Use SERIAL to auto-generate primary keys

evidence_span.text: > CREATE TABLE serial (a SERIAL PRIMARY KEY, b STRING, c BOOL);

supporting_evidence.section_heading: SERIAL / ​ Example / ​ Use SERIAL to auto-generate primary keys

evidence_span.text: The JSONB stores JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) data as a binary representation of the JSONB value, which eliminates whitespace, duplicate keys, and key ordering. JSONB supports .

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSONB

evidence_span.text: ​ Alias

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSONB

evidence_span.text: In CockroachDB, JSON is an alias for JSONB .

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSONB / ​ Alias

evidence_span.text: ​ Syntax

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSONB / ​ Alias

evidence_span.text: The syntax for the JSONB data type follows the format specified in RFC8259 . You can express a constant value of type JSONB using an or a string literal type JSONB .

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSONB / ​ Alias / ​ Syntax

evidence_span.text: There are six types of JSONB values:

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSONB / ​ Alias / ​ Syntax

evidence_span.text: null

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSONB / ​ Alias / ​ Syntax

evidence_span.text: Boolean

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSONB / ​ Alias / ​ Syntax

evidence_span.text: String

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSONB / ​ Alias / ​ Syntax

evidence_span.text: Number (i.e., , not the standard int64 )

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSONB / ​ Alias / ​ Syntax

evidence_span.text: Array (i.e., an ordered sequence of JSONB values)

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSONB / ​ Alias / ​ Syntax

evidence_span.text: Object (i.e., a mapping from strings to JSONB values)

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSONB / ​ Alias / ​ Syntax

evidence_span.text: ​ Size

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSONB

evidence_span.text: The size of a JSONB value is variable, but we recommend that you keep values under 1 MB to ensure satisfactory performance. Above that threshold, and other considerations may cause significant performance degradation.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSONB / ​ Size

evidence_span.text: We strongly recommend adding size limits to all , which includes columns in .

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSONB / ​ Size

evidence_span.text: Values exceeding 1 MiB can lead to and cause significant performance degradation or even .

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSONB / ​ Size

evidence_span.text: To add a size limit using :

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSONB / ​ Size

evidence_span.text: CREATE TABLE name (first STRING(100), last STRING(100));

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSONB / ​ Size

evidence_span.text: To add a size limit using :

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSONB / ​ Size

evidence_span.text: ALTER TABLE name ALTER first TYPE STRING(99);

evidence_span.text: Operator Description Example Query and Output -> Access a JSONB field, returning a JSONB value. SELECT '[{"foo":"bar"}]'::JSONB->0->'foo'; "bar"::JSONB ->> Access a JSONB field, returning a string. SELECT '{"foo":"bar"}'::JSONB->>'foo'; bar::STRING @> Tests whether the left JSONB field contains the right JSONB field. SELECT ('{"foo": {"baz": 3}, "bar": 2}'::JSONB@>'{"foo": {"baz":3}}'::JSONB ); true <@ Tests whether the left JSONB field is contained by the right JSONB field. SELECT('{"bar":2}'::JSONB<@'{"foo":1, "bar":2}'::JSONB); true #> Access a JSONB field at the specified path, returning a JSONB value. SELECT '[{"foo":"bar"}]'::JSONB#>'{0,foo}'; "bar"::JSONB #>> Access a JSONB field at the specified path, returning a string. SELECT '[{"foo":"bar"}]'::JSONB#>>'{0,foo}'; bar::STRING ? Does the key or element string exist within the JSONB value? SELECT('{"foo":1, "bar":2}'::JSONB?'bar'); true ?& Do all the key or element strings exist within the JSONB value? SELECT('{"foo":1, "bar":2}'::JSONB?&array['foo','bar']); true ?| Do any of the key or element strings exist within the JSONB value? SELECT('{"foo":1, "bar":2}'::JSONB?|array['bar']); true [ … ] Access a JSONB key, returning a JSONB value or object. For details, see . SELECT('{"foo": {"bar":1}}'::JSONB)['foo']['bar']; 1

evidence_span.text: To retrieve JSONB data with easier-to-read formatting, use the jsonb_pretty() function. For example, retrieve data from the table you created in the first example :

evidence_span.text: ​ Retrieve a specific field from JSONB data

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSONB / ​ Examples

evidence_span.text: To retrieve a specific field from JSONB data, use the -> operator. For example, to retrieve a field from the table you created in Create a table with a JSONB column , run:

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSONB / ​ Examples / ​ Retrieve a specific field from JSONB data

evidence_span.text: SELECT user_profile->'first_name',user_profile->'location' FROM users;

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSONB / ​ Examples / ​ Retrieve a specific field from JSONB data

evidence_span.text:
?column? |  ?column?
-----------+-------------
  "Ernie"  | "Brooklyn"
  "Lola"   | "NYC"

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSONB / ​ Examples / ​ Retrieve a specific field from JSONB data

evidence_span.text: You can also use a for an equivalent result:

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSONB / ​ Examples / ​ Retrieve a specific field from JSONB data

evidence_span.text: SELECT (user_profile)['first_name'],(user_profile)['location'] FROM users;

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSONB / ​ Examples / ​ Retrieve a specific field from JSONB data

evidence_span.text:
user_profile | user_profile
---------------+---------------
  "Ernie"      | "Brooklyn"
  "Lola"       | "NYC"

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSONB / ​ Examples / ​ Retrieve a specific field from JSONB data

evidence_span.text: Use the ->> operator to return JSONB fields as STRING values:

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSONB / ​ Examples / ​ Retrieve a specific field from JSONB data

evidence_span.text: SELECT user_profile->>'first_name', user_profile->>'location' FROM users;

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSONB / ​ Examples / ​ Retrieve a specific field from JSONB data

evidence_span.text:
?column? | ?column?
-----------+-----------
  Ernie    | Brooklyn
  Lola     | NYC

evidence_span.text: Use the @> operator to filter the values in a field in a JSONB column:

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSONB / ​ Examples / ​ Retrieve a specific field from JSONB data

evidence_span.text: SELECT user_profile->'first_name', user_profile->'location' FROM users WHERE user_profile @> '{"location":"NYC"}';

evidence_span.text: ​ Group and order JSONB values

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSONB / ​ Examples

evidence_span.text: To organize your JSONB field values, use the GROUP BY and ORDER BY clauses with the ->> operator. For example, organize the first_name values from the table you created in the first example :

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSONB / ​ Examples / ​ Group and order JSONB values

evidence_span.text: For this example, we will add a few more records to the existing table. This will help us see clearly how the data is grouped.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSONB / ​ Examples / ​ Group and order JSONB values
JSONB / ​ Examples / ​ Group and order JSONB values

evidence_span.text: SELECT user_profile->>'first_name' AS first_name, user_profile->>'location' AS location FROM users;

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSONB / ​ Examples / ​ Group and order JSONB values

evidence_span.text:
first_name | location
-------------+-----------
  Ernie      | Brooklyn
  Lola       | NYC
  Parvati    | London
  Lola       | Seoul

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSONB / ​ Examples / ​ Group and order JSONB values

evidence_span.text: Group and order the data.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSONB / ​ Examples / ​ Group and order JSONB values

evidence_span.text: SELECT user_profile->>'first_name' first_name, count(*) total FROM users group by user_profile->>'first_name' order by total;

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSONB / ​ Examples / ​ Group and order JSONB values

evidence_span.text:
first_name | total
-------------+-------
  Ernie      | 1
  Parvati    | 1
  Lola       | 2

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSONB / ​ Examples / ​ Group and order JSONB values

evidence_span.text: In this example, create a table with a JSONB column and a stored computed column:

evidence_span.text: Create a compute column after you create a table:

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSONB / ​ Examples / ​ Create a table with a JSONB column and a computed column

evidence_span.text: > ALTER TABLE student_profiles ADD COLUMN age INT AS ( (profile->>'age')::INT) STORED;

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSONB / ​ Examples / ​ Create a table with a JSONB column and a computed column

evidence_span.text: Then, insert a few rows of data:

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSONB / ​ Examples / ​ Create a table with a JSONB column and a computed column

evidence_span.text:
> INSERT INTO student_profiles (profile) VALUES
    ('{"id": "d78236", "name": "Arthur Read", "age": "16", "school": "PVPHS", "credits": 120, "sports": "none"}'),
    ('{"name": "Buster Bunny", "age": "15", "id": "f98112", "school": "THS", "credits": 67, "clubs": "MUN"}'),
    ('{"name": "Ernie Narayan", "school" : "Brooklyn Tech", "id": "t63512", "sports": "Track and Field", "clubs": "Chess"}');

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSONB / ​ Examples / ​ Create a table with a JSONB column and a computed column

evidence_span.text: > SELECT * FROM student_profiles;

JSONB / ​ Examples / ​ Create a table with a JSONB column and a computed column

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSONB / ​ Examples

evidence_span.text: In this example, create a table with a JSONB column and virtual computed columns:

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSONB / ​ Examples / ​ Create a table with a JSONB column and a virtual computed column
JSONB / ​ Examples / ​ Create a table with a JSONB column and a virtual computed column

evidence_span.text: Then, insert a few rows of data:

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSONB / ​ Examples / ​ Create a table with a JSONB column and a virtual computed column

evidence_span.text:
> INSERT INTO student_profiles (profile) VALUES
    ('{"id": "d78236", "firstName": "Arthur", "lastName": "Read", "birthdate": "2010-01-25", "school": "PVPHS", "credits": 120, "sports": "none"}'),
    ('{"firstName": "Buster", "lastName": "Bunny", "birthdate": "2011-11-07", "id": "f98112", "school": "THS", "credits": 67, "clubs": "MUN"}'),
    ('{"firstName": "Ernie", "lastName": "Narayan", "school" : "Brooklyn Tech", "id": "t63512", "sports": "Track and Field", "clubs": "Chess"}');

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSONB / ​ Examples / ​ Create a table with a JSONB column and a virtual computed column

evidence_span.text: > SELECT * FROM student_profiles;

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSONB / ​ Examples / ​ Create a table with a JSONB column and a virtual computed column
JSONB / ​ Examples / ​ Create a table with a JSONB column and a virtual computed column

evidence_span.text: The virtual column full_name is computed as a field from the profile column’s data. The first name and last name are concatenated and separated by a single whitespace character using the .

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSONB / ​ Examples / ​ Create a table with a JSONB column and a virtual computed column

evidence_span.text: The virtual column birthday is parsed as a TIMESTAMP value from the profile column’s birthdate string value. The is used to parse strings in TIMESTAMP format.

evidence_span.text: This section describes how to cast and convert JSONB values.

evidence_span.text: You can all JSONB values to the following data type:

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSONB / ​ Supported casting and conversion

evidence_span.text: You can cast numeric JSONB values to the following numeric data types:

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSONB / ​ Supported casting and conversion

evidence_span.text: For example:

evidence_span.text: SELECT '100'::JSONB::INT;

evidence_span.text: You can use the to parse strings in TIMESTAMP format.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSONB / ​ Supported casting and conversion

evidence_span.text: SELECT parse_timestamp ('2022-05-28T10:53:25.160Z');

evidence_span.text: st_azimuth(geography_a: geography, geography_b: geography) -> float Returns the azimuth in radians of the segment defined by the given point geographies, or NULL if the two points are coincident. It is solved using the Inverse geodesic problem. The azimuth is angle is referenced from north, and is positive clockwise: North = 0; East = π/2; South = π; West = 3π/2. This function utilizes the GeographicLib library for spheroid calculations. Immutable

supporting_evidence.section_heading: DATE

evidence_span.text: The DATE stores a year, month, and day.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: DATE

evidence_span.text: ​ Syntax

supporting_evidence.section_heading: DATE

evidence_span.text: You can express a constant value of type DATE using an , or a string literal type DATE or type DATE .

supporting_evidence.section_heading: DATE / ​ Syntax

evidence_span.text: CockroachDB also supports using uninterpreted in contexts where a DATE value is otherwise expected. By default, CockroachDB parses the following string formats for dates:

supporting_evidence.section_heading: DATE / ​ Syntax

evidence_span.text: YYYY-MM-DD

supporting_evidence.section_heading: DATE / ​ Syntax

evidence_span.text: MM-DD-YYYY

supporting_evidence.section_heading: DATE / ​ Syntax

evidence_span.text: MM-DD-YY (default)/ YY-MM-DD / DD-MM-YY

supporting_evidence.section_heading: DATE / ​ Syntax

evidence_span.text: To change the input format of truncated dates (e.g., 12-16-06 ) from MM-DD-YY to YY-MM-DD or DD-MM-YY , set the datestyle or the sql.defaults.datestyle .

supporting_evidence.section_heading: DATE / ​ Syntax

evidence_span.text: Use instead of the sql.defaults.* . This allows you to set a default value for all users for any that applies during login, making the sql.defaults.* cluster settings redundant.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: DATE / ​ Syntax

evidence_span.text: ​ PostgreSQL compatibility

supporting_evidence.section_heading: DATE

evidence_span.text: DATE values in CockroachDB are fully PostgreSQL-compatible , including support for special values (e.g., +/- infinity ). Existing dates outside of the PostgreSQL date range ( 4714-11-24 BC to 5874897-12-31 ) are converted to +/- infinity dates.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: DATE / ​ PostgreSQL compatibility

evidence_span.text: ​ Size

supporting_evidence.section_heading: DATE

evidence_span.text: A DATE column supports values up to 16 bytes in width, but the total storage size is likely to be larger due to CockroachDB metadata.

The cost parameters specify how much to charge for each edit operation. If actual distance is less or equal then max_d, then it returns the distance. supporting_evidence.section_heading: UUID

evidence_span.text: The UUID (Universally Unique Identifier) implements the UUIDv4 format from RFC 4122 . It stores a 128-bit value that is “unique across both space and time, with respect to the space of all UUIDs” as specified by the RFC.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: UUID

evidence_span.text: To auto-generate UUIDs:

supporting_evidence.section_heading: UUID

evidence_span.text: Use the gen_random_uuid() function as the default value of the UUID data type.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: UUID

evidence_span.text: Use the uuid_v4() function as the default value of the data type.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: UUID

evidence_span.text: For examples, refer to Create a table with auto-generated unique row IDs .

supporting_evidence.section_heading: UUID

evidence_span.text: For performance reasons, if you are going to use UUIDs, Cockroach Labs strongly recommends using UUIDv4 as defined by RFC 4122 . This is the format generated by the . Other types of UUID are largely untested with CockroachDB and will require performance testing to avoid .

supporting_evidence.section_heading: UUID

evidence_span.text: ​ Syntax

supporting_evidence.section_heading: UUID

evidence_span.text: You can express UUID values using the following formats:

supporting_evidence.section_heading: UUID / ​ Syntax

evidence_span.text: Format Description Standard RFC4122 (UUIDv4) format Hyphen-separated groups of 8, 4, 4, 4, and 12 hexadecimal digits. Example: acde070d-8c4c-4f0d-9d8a-162843c10333 BYTES UUID value specified as a value. Example: b'kafef00ddeadbeed' Uniform Resource Name A Uniform Resource Name (URN) specified as “urn:uuid:” followed by the RFC4122 format. Example: urn:uuid:63616665-6630-3064-6465-616462656564 Alternate PostgreSQL-supported formats All alternate UUID formats supported by PostgreSQL , including the RFC4122 format surrounded by braces, any supported format with upper-case digits, any supported format with some or all hyphens omitted, and any supported format with hyphens after any group of four digits. Examples: , ACDE070D-8C4C-4f0D-9d8A-162843c10333 , acde070d8c4c4f0d9d8a162843c10333 , acde-070d-8c4c-4f0d-9d8a-1628-43c1-0333

);

UUID / ​ Examples / ​ Create a table with auto-generated unique row IDs / ​ Use uuid_v4()

evidence_span.text: In either case, generated IDs will be 128-bit, sufficiently large to generate unique values. Once the table grows beyond a single key-value range’s , new IDs will be scattered across all of the table’s ranges and, therefore, likely across different nodes. This means that multiple nodes will share in the load.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: UUID / ​ Examples / ​ Create a table with auto-generated unique row IDs / ​ Use uuid_v4()

evidence_span.text: This approach has the disadvantage of creating a primary key that may not be useful in a query directly, which can require a join with another table or a secondary index.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: UUID / ​ Examples / ​ Create a table with auto-generated unique row IDs / ​ Use uuid_v4()

evidence_span.text: ​ Use unique_rowid()

supporting_evidence.section_heading: UUID / ​ Examples / ​ Create a table with auto-generated unique row IDs

evidence_span.text: If it is important for generated IDs to be stored in the same key-value range, you can use an with the unique_rowid() as the default value, either explicitly or via the :

supporting_evidence.section_heading: UUID / ​ Examples / ​ Create a table with auto-generated unique row IDs / ​ Use unique_rowid()

evidence_span.text:
CREATE TABLE users3 (
    id INT DEFAULT unique_rowid(),
    city STRING NOT NULL,
    name STRING NULL,
    address STRING NULL,
    credit_card STRING NULL,
    CONSTRAINT "primary" PRIMARY KEY (city ASC, id ASC),
    FAMILY "primary" (id, city, name, address, credit_card)
);

supporting_evidence.section_heading: UUID / ​ Examples / ​ Create a table with auto-generated unique row IDs / ​ Use unique_rowid()

evidence_span.text: INSERT INTO users3 (name, city) VALUES ('Blake', 'chicago'), ('Hannah', 'seattle'), ('Bobby', 'seattle');

supporting_evidence.section_heading: UUID / ​ Examples / ​ Create a table with auto-generated unique row IDs / ​ Use unique_rowid()

evidence_span.text: SELECT * FROM users3;

supporting_evidence.section_heading: UUID / ​ Examples / ​ Create a table with auto-generated unique row IDs / ​ Use unique_rowid()
UUID / ​ Examples / ​ Create a table with auto-generated unique row IDs / ​ Use unique_rowid()

evidence_span.text: Upon insert or upsert, the unique_rowid() function generates a default value from the timestamp and ID of the node executing the insert. Such time-ordered values are likely to be globally unique except in cases where a very large number of IDs (100,000+) are generated per node per second. Also, there can be gaps and the order is not completely guaranteed.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: UUID / ​ Examples / ​ Create a table with auto-generated unique row IDs / ​ Use unique_rowid()

evidence_span.text: In multi-region deployments with tables, uniqueness checks can add latency due to cross-partition validation. You can improve performance by setting the skip_unique_checks index storage parameter to true , but this is only recommended if the application can guarantee uniqueness. For more information, refer to .

supporting_evidence.section_heading: UUID / ​ Examples / ​ Create a table with auto-generated unique row IDs / ​ Use unique_rowid()

evidence_span.text: To understand the differences between the UUID and unique_rowid() options, see the . For further background on UUIDs, see What is a UUID, and Why Should You Care? .

This function utilizes the GeographicLib library for spheroid calculations. Immutable

evidence_span.text: The DECIMAL stores exact, fixed-point numbers. This type is used when it is important to preserve exact precision, for example, with monetary data.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: DECIMAL

evidence_span.text: ​ Aliases

supporting_evidence.section_heading: DECIMAL

evidence_span.text: In CockroachDB, the following are aliases for DECIMAL :

supporting_evidence.section_heading: DECIMAL / ​ Aliases

evidence_span.text: DEC

supporting_evidence.section_heading: DECIMAL / ​ Aliases

evidence_span.text: NUMERIC

supporting_evidence.section_heading: DECIMAL / ​ Aliases

evidence_span.text: ​ Precision and scale

supporting_evidence.section_heading: DECIMAL

evidence_span.text: To limit a decimal column, use DECIMAL(precision, scale) , where precision is the maximum count of digits both to the left and right of the decimal point and scale is the exact count of digits to the right of the decimal point. The precision must not be smaller than the scale . Also note that using DECIMAL(precision) is equivalent to DECIMAL(precision, 0) .

supporting_evidence.section_heading: DECIMAL / ​ Precision and scale

evidence_span.text: When inserting a decimal value:

supporting_evidence.section_heading: DECIMAL / ​ Precision and scale

evidence_span.text: If digits to the right of the decimal point exceed the column’s scale , CockroachDB rounds to the scale.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: DECIMAL / ​ Precision and scale

evidence_span.text: If digits to the right of the decimal point are fewer than the column’s scale , CockroachDB pads to the scale with 0 s.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: DECIMAL / ​ Precision and scale

evidence_span.text: If digits to the left and right of the decimal point exceed the column’s precision , CockroachDB gives an error.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: DECIMAL / ​ Precision and scale

evidence_span.text: If the column’s precision and scale are identical, the inserted value must round to less than 1.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: DECIMAL / ​ Precision and scale

evidence_span.text: ​ Syntax

supporting_evidence.section_heading: DECIMAL

evidence_span.text: A constant value of type DECIMAL can be entered as a . For example: 1.414 or -1234 .

supporting_evidence.section_heading: DECIMAL / ​ Syntax

evidence_span.text: The special IEEE754 values for positive infinity, negative infinity and NaN (Not-a-Number) cannot be entered using numeric literals directly and must be converted using an or an from a string literal instead.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: DECIMAL / ​ Syntax

evidence_span.text: The following values are recognized:

supporting_evidence.section_heading: DECIMAL / ​ Syntax

evidence_span.text: Syntax Value inf , infinity , +inf , +infinity +∞ -inf , -infinity -∞ nan NaN (Not-a-Number)

evidence_span.text: The TSQUERY stores a list of lexemes separated by operators. TSQUERY values are used in .

evidence_span.text: ​ Syntax

supporting_evidence.section_heading: TSQUERY

evidence_span.text: A TSQUERY comprises individual lexemes and operators in the form: 'These' & 'lexemes' & 'are' & 'not' & 'normalized' & 'lexemes.' .

supporting_evidence.section_heading: TSQUERY / ​ Syntax

evidence_span.text: The operators in a TSQUERY are used to . Valid TSQUERY operators are:

supporting_evidence.section_heading: TSQUERY / ​ Syntax

evidence_span.text: & (AND). Given 'one' & 'two' , both one and two must be present in the matching TSVECTOR .

supporting_evidence.section_heading: TSQUERY / ​ Syntax

evidence_span.text: | (OR). Given 'one' | 'two' , either one or two must be present in the matching TSVECTOR .

supporting_evidence.section_heading: TSQUERY / ​ Syntax

evidence_span.text: ! (NOT). Given 'one' & ! 'two' , one must be present and two must not be present in the matching TSVECTOR .

supporting_evidence.section_heading: TSQUERY / ​ Syntax

evidence_span.text: (FOLLOWED BY). Given

supporting_evidence.section_heading: TSQUERY / ​ Syntax

evidence_span.text: 'one' <-> 'two'

supporting_evidence.section_heading: TSQUERY / ​ Syntax
TSQUERY / ​ Syntax

evidence_span.text: one

supporting_evidence.section_heading: TSQUERY / ​ Syntax

evidence_span.text: must be followed by

supporting_evidence.section_heading: TSQUERY / ​ Syntax

evidence_span.text: two

supporting_evidence.section_heading: TSQUERY / ​ Syntax

evidence_span.text: in the matching

supporting_evidence.section_heading: TSQUERY / ​ Syntax

evidence_span.text: TSVECTOR

supporting_evidence.section_heading: TSQUERY / ​ Syntax
TSQUERY / ​ Syntax

evidence_span.text: <-> is equivalent to <1> . You can specify an integer <n to indicate that lexemes must be separated by n-1 other lexemes. Given 'one' <4> 'two' , one must be followed by three lexemes and then followed by two in the matching TSVECTOR .

supporting_evidence.section_heading: TSQUERY / ​ Syntax

evidence_span.text: You can optionally add the following to each lexeme:

supporting_evidence.section_heading: TSQUERY / ​ Syntax

evidence_span.text: One or more weight letters ( A , B , C , or D ): 'These' & 'lexemes':B & 'are' & 'not' & 'normalized':A & 'lexemes':B If not specified, a lexeme’s weight defaults to D . It is only necessary to specify weights in a TSQUERY if they are also to be used in a comparison. The lexemes in a TSQUERY and TSVECTOR will only match if they have matching weights. For more information about weights, see the PostgreSQL documentation .

supporting_evidence.section_heading: TSQUERY / ​ Syntax

evidence_span.text: To be usable in , the lexemes must be normalized . You can do this by using the to_tsquery() , plainto_tsquery() , or phraseto_tsquery() to convert a string input to TSQUERY :

supporting_evidence.section_heading: TSQUERY / ​ Syntax

evidence_span.text: SELECT to_tsquery('These & lexemes & are & not & normalized & lexemes.');

evidence_span.text: Stop words . These are words that are considered not useful for indexing and searching, based on the . In the preceding example, “These”, “are”, and “not” are identified as stop words.

evidence_span.text: CockroachDB supports precision levels from 0 (seconds) to 6 (microseconds) for TIMESTAMP / TIMESTAMPTZ values. Precision in time values specifies the number of fractional digits retained in the seconds field. For example, specifying a TIMESTAMPTZ value as TIMESTAMPTZ(3) truncates the time component to milliseconds. By default, TIMESTAMP / TIMESTAMPTZ values have a precision of 6 (microseconds).

evidence_span.text: You can use an statement to change the precision level of a TIMESTAMP / TIMESTAMPTZ -typed column. If there is already a non-default precision level specified for the column, the precision level can only be changed to an equal or greater precision level. For an example, see Create a table with a TIMESTAMP -typed column, with precision .

supporting_evidence.section_heading: TIMESTAMP / TIMESTAMPTZ

evidence_span.text: The TIMESTAMP and TIMESTAMPTZ store a date and time pair in UTC.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: TIMESTAMP / TIMESTAMPTZ

evidence_span.text: ​ Variants

supporting_evidence.section_heading: TIMESTAMP / TIMESTAMPTZ

evidence_span.text: TIMESTAMP has two variants:

supporting_evidence.section_heading: TIMESTAMP / TIMESTAMPTZ / ​ Variants

evidence_span.text: TIMESTAMP presents all TIMESTAMP values in UTC.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: TIMESTAMP / TIMESTAMPTZ / ​ Variants

evidence_span.text: TIMESTAMPTZ converts TIMESTAMP values from UTC to the client’s session time zone (unless another time zone is specified for the value). However, it is conceptually important to note that TIMESTAMPTZ does not store any time zone data.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: TIMESTAMP / TIMESTAMPTZ / ​ Variants

evidence_span.text: The default session time zone is UTC, which means that by default TIMESTAMPTZ values display in UTC.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: TIMESTAMP / TIMESTAMPTZ / ​ Variants

evidence_span.text: The difference between these two variants is that TIMESTAMPTZ uses the client’s session , while the other simply does not. This behavior extends to functions like now() and extract() on TIMESTAMPTZ values.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: TIMESTAMP / TIMESTAMPTZ / ​ Variants

evidence_span.text: A time zone offset of +00:00 is displayed for all and TIMESTAMP values, but is not stored in the database.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: TIMESTAMP / TIMESTAMPTZ / ​ Variants

evidence_span.text: You can use the and functions to convert a TIMESTAMPTZ into a TIMESTAMP at a specified timezone, or to convert a TIMESTAMP into a TIMESTAMPTZ at a specified timezone.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: TIMESTAMP / TIMESTAMPTZ / ​ Variants

evidence_span.text: Explore the differences of TIMESTAMP and TIMESTAMPTZ in the following video:

supporting_evidence.section_heading: TIMESTAMP / TIMESTAMPTZ / ​ Variants

evidence_span.text: ​ Best practices

supporting_evidence.section_heading: TIMESTAMP / TIMESTAMPTZ

evidence_span.text: We recommend always using the TIMESTAMPTZ variant because the TIMESTAMP variant can sometimes lead to unexpected behaviors when it ignores a session offset. However, we also recommend you avoid for your database.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: TIMESTAMP / TIMESTAMPTZ / ​ Best practices

evidence_span.text: ​ Aliases

supporting_evidence.section_heading: TIMESTAMP / TIMESTAMPTZ

evidence_span.text: In CockroachDB, the following are aliases:

supporting_evidence.section_heading: TIMESTAMP / TIMESTAMPTZ / ​ Aliases

evidence_span.text: TIMESTAMP , TIMESTAMP WITHOUT TIME ZONE

supporting_evidence.section_heading: TIMESTAMP / TIMESTAMPTZ / ​ Aliases

evidence_span.text: TIMESTAMPTZ , TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE

supporting_evidence.section_heading: TIMESTAMP / TIMESTAMPTZ / ​ Aliases

evidence_span.text: ​ Syntax

supporting_evidence.section_heading: TIMESTAMP / TIMESTAMPTZ

evidence_span.text: You can express a constant value of type TIMESTAMP / TIMESTAMPTZ using an , or a string literal type TIMESTAMP / TIMESTAMPTZ or type TIMESTAMP / TIMESTAMPTZ . When it is unambiguous, a simple unannotated is automatically interpreted as type TIMESTAMP or TIMESTAMPTZ .

supporting_evidence.section_heading: TIMESTAMP / TIMESTAMPTZ / ​ Syntax

evidence_span.text: You can express TIMESTAMP constants using the following string literal formats:

supporting_evidence.section_heading: TIMESTAMP / TIMESTAMPTZ / ​ Syntax

evidence_span.text: Format Example Date only TIMESTAMP '2016-01-25' Date and Time TIMESTAMP '2016-01-25 10:10:10.555555' ISO 8601 TIMESTAMP '2016-01-25T10:10:10.555555'

supporting_evidence.section_heading: TIMESTAMP / TIMESTAMPTZ / ​ Syntax

evidence_span.text: Format Example

supporting_evidence.section_heading: TIMESTAMP / TIMESTAMPTZ / ​ Syntax

evidence_span.text: Date only TIMESTAMP '2016-01-25'

supporting_evidence.section_heading: TIMESTAMP / TIMESTAMPTZ / ​ Syntax

evidence_span.text: Date and Time TIMESTAMP '2016-01-25 10:10:10.555555'

supporting_evidence.section_heading: TIMESTAMP / TIMESTAMPTZ / ​ Syntax
TIMESTAMP / TIMESTAMPTZ / ​ Syntax

evidence_span.text: To express a TIMESTAMPTZ value with time zone offset from UTC, use the following format: TIMESTAMPTZ '2016-01-25 10:10:10.555555-05:00' . The fractional portion is optional and is rounded to microseconds (6 digits after decimal) for compatibility with the PostgreSQL wire protocol.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: TIMESTAMP / TIMESTAMPTZ / ​ Syntax

evidence_span.text: By default, CockroachDB interprets truncated dates (e.g., 12-16-06 ) as MM-DD-YY . To change the input string format of truncated dates, set the datestyle or the sql.defaults.datestyle .

supporting_evidence.section_heading: TIMESTAMP / TIMESTAMPTZ / ​ Syntax

evidence_span.text: Use instead of the sql.defaults.* . This allows you to set a default value for all users for any that applies during login, making the sql.defaults.* cluster settings redundant.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: TIMESTAMP / TIMESTAMPTZ / ​ Syntax

evidence_span.text: ​ Size

supporting_evidence.section_heading: TIMESTAMP / TIMESTAMPTZ

evidence_span.text: A TIMESTAMP / TIMESTAMPTZ column supports values up to 12 bytes in width, but the total storage size is likely to be larger due to CockroachDB metadata.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: TIMESTAMP / TIMESTAMPTZ / ​ Size

evidence_span.text: ​ Precision

supporting_evidence.section_heading: TIMESTAMP / TIMESTAMPTZ

evidence_span.text: CockroachDB supports precision levels from 0 (seconds) to 6 (microseconds) for TIMESTAMP / TIMESTAMPTZ values. Precision in time values specifies the number of fractional digits retained in the seconds field. For example, specifying a TIMESTAMPTZ value as TIMESTAMPTZ(3) truncates the time component to milliseconds. By default, TIMESTAMP / TIMESTAMPTZ values have a precision of 6 (microseconds).

supporting_evidence.section_heading: TIMESTAMP / TIMESTAMPTZ / ​ Precision

evidence_span.text: You can use an statement to change the precision level of a TIMESTAMP / TIMESTAMPTZ -typed column. If there is already a non-default precision level specified for the column, the precision level can only be changed to an equal or greater precision level. For an example, see Create a table with a TIMESTAMP -typed column, with precision .

supporting_evidence.section_heading: TIMESTAMP / TIMESTAMPTZ / ​ Precision

evidence_span.text: ​ Supported casting and conversion

supporting_evidence.section_heading: TIMESTAMP / TIMESTAMPTZ

evidence_span.text: TIMESTAMP values can be to any of the following data types:

supporting_evidence.section_heading: TIMESTAMP / TIMESTAMPTZ / ​ Supported casting and conversion

evidence_span.text: Type Details DECIMAL Converts to number of seconds since the Unix epoch (Jan. 1, 1970). FLOAT Converts to number of seconds since the Unix epoch (Jan. 1, 1970). TIME Converts to the time portion ( HH:MM:SS ) of the timestamp. INT Converts to number of seconds since the Unix epoch (Jan. 1, 1970). DATE Converts to the date ( YYYY-MM-DD ) of the timestamp and omits the other information. STRING Converts to the date and time portion ( YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS ) of the timestamp and omits the time zone offset.

evidence_span.text: ​ Infinity TIMESTAMP casts

supporting_evidence.section_heading: TIMESTAMP / TIMESTAMPTZ / ​ Supported casting and conversion

evidence_span.text: CockroachDB does not support an infinity / -infinity representation for TIMESTAMP casts. Instead, infinity::TIMESTAMP evaluates to 294276-12-31 23:59:59.999999+00:00 , the maximum TIMESTAMP value supported, and -infinity::TIMESTAMP evaluates to -4714-11-24 00:00:00+00:00 , the minimum TIMESTAMP value supported.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: TIMESTAMP / TIMESTAMPTZ / ​ Supported casting and conversion / ​ Infinity TIMESTAMP casts

evidence_span.text: Note that this behavior differs from PostgreSQL, for which infinity is higher than any allowable TIMESTAMP value (including 294276-12-31 23:59:59.999999+00:00 ), and -infinity is lower than any allowable TIMESTAMP value (including -4714-11-24 00:00:00+00:00 ).

evidence_span.text: pg_indexes_size(relation_oid: oid) -> int Returns the total on-disk size, in bytes, of the secondary indexes attached to the relation with the given OID. The primary index is excluded (it is reported by pg_relation_size and pg_table_size, since CockroachDB stores row data in the primary index). The size is read from a periodically-refreshed cache and may lag behind the true value by minutes. Returns NULL if no such relation exists or has no on-disk representation. Volatile

evidence_span.text: _st_dwithinexclusive(geography_a: geography, geography_b: geography, distance: float ) -> bool Returns true if any of geography_a is within distance meters of geography_b, exclusive. Uses a spheroid to perform the operation. When operating on a spheroid, this function will use the sphere to calculate the closest two points. The spheroid distance between these two points is calculated using GeographicLib. This follows observed PostGIS behavior. The calculations performed are have a precision of 1cm. This function utilizes the GeographicLib library for spheroid calculations. This function variant does not utilize any spatial index. Immutable

supporting_evidence.section_heading: FLOAT

evidence_span.text: CockroachDB supports various inexact, floating-point number with up to 17 digits of decimal precision.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: FLOAT

evidence_span.text: They are handled internally using the standard double-precision (64-bit binary-encoded) IEEE754 format .

supporting_evidence.section_heading: FLOAT

evidence_span.text: ​ Syntax

supporting_evidence.section_heading: FLOAT

evidence_span.text: A constant value of type FLOAT can be entered as a . For example: 1.414 or -1234 .

supporting_evidence.section_heading: FLOAT / ​ Syntax

evidence_span.text: The special IEEE754 values for positive infinity, negative infinity and NaN (Not-a-Number) cannot be entered using numeric literals directly and must be converted using an or an from a string literal instead.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: FLOAT / ​ Syntax

evidence_span.text: The following values are recognized:

supporting_evidence.section_heading: FLOAT / ​ Syntax

evidence_span.text: ​ Supported casting and conversion

supporting_evidence.section_heading: FLOAT

evidence_span.text: FLOAT values can be to any of the following data types:

supporting_evidence.section_heading: FLOAT / ​ Supported casting and conversion

evidence_span.text: Type Details INT Rounds the float to the nearest integer. If equidistant to two integers, rounds to the even integer. See Cast FLOAT to INT . DECIMAL Causes an error to be reported if the value is NaN or +/- Inf. BOOL 0 converts to false ; any other value converts to true . STRING —

evidence_span.text: ​ Cast FLOAT to INT

supporting_evidence.section_heading: FLOAT / ​ Supported casting and conversion

evidence_span.text: If you cast a float to an integer, it is rounded to the nearest integer. If it is equidistant to two integers, it is rounded to the even integer.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: FLOAT / ​ Supported casting and conversion / ​ Cast FLOAT to INT

evidence_span.text: For example:

supporting_evidence.section_heading: FLOAT / ​ Supported casting and conversion / ​ Cast FLOAT to INT

evidence_span.text: SELECT f::INT FROM (VALUES (-1.5::FLOAT), (-0.5::FLOAT), (0.5::FLOAT), (1.5::FLOAT)) v(f);

evidence_span.text: follower_read_timestamp() -> timestamptz Returns a timestamp which is very likely to be safe to perform against a follower replica. This function is intended to be used with an AS OF SYSTEM TIME clause to perform historical reads against a time which is recent but sufficiently old for reads to be performed against the closest replica as opposed to the currently leaseholder for a given range. Note that this function requires an enterprise license on a CCL distribution to return a result that is less likely the closest replica. It is otherwise hardcoded as -4.8s from the statement time, which may not result in reading from the nearest replica. Volatile

evidence_span.text: CockroachDB supports duration fields for INTERVAL values. You can specify SECOND , MINUTE , HOUR , or DAY units of duration in the form INTERVAL ... <unit> or INTERVAL ... <unit> TO <unit> .
