source_locations.dom_locator: html > body > div#root > div > div > div > div > main#content-container > div > div#content-area > div#content > span:nth-of-type(10)

description.value: CockroachDB supports duration fields for INTERVAL values. You can specify SECOND , MINUTE , HOUR , or DAY units of duration in the form INTERVAL ... <unit> or INTERVAL ... <unit> TO <unit> .

evidence_span.text: Specifying a single duration field truncates the interval at the unit specified, defining the interval as having the duration field unit as its least-significant unit. For example, INTERVAL '1 2:03:04' HOUR truncates the input to an exact hour, and parses the interval as 1 day 02:00:00 .

evidence_span.text: A single duration field can also resolve ambiguity in the input. For example, INTERVAL '1' parses the interval as 00:00:01 (1 second). INTERVAL '1' MINUTE parses the interval as 00:01:00 (1 minute).

description.value: A single duration field can also resolve ambiguity in the input. For example, INTERVAL '1' parses the interval as 00:00:01 (1 second). INTERVAL '1' MINUTE parses the interval as 00:01:00 (1 minute).

evidence_span.text: If the interval input is ambiguous, specifying two duration fields stores the interval in the units specified. For example, INTERVAL '02:03' MINUTE TO SECOND parses the interval as 00:02:03 (in minutes and seconds). Without MINUTE TO SECOND , the input would be parsed as 02:03:00 (in hours and minutes).

supporting_evidence.section_heading: INTERVAL

evidence_span.text: The INTERVAL stores a value that represents a span of time.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: INTERVAL

evidence_span.text: ​ Syntax

supporting_evidence.section_heading: INTERVAL

evidence_span.text: You can express a constant value of type INTERVAL using an , or a string literal type INTERVAL or type INTERVAL . CockroachDB also supports using uninterpreted in contexts where an INTERVAL value is otherwise expected.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: INTERVAL / ​ Syntax

evidence_span.text: INTERVAL constants can be expressed using the following formats:

supporting_evidence.section_heading: INTERVAL / ​ Syntax

evidence_span.text: Format Description SQL Standard INTERVAL 'Y-M D H:M:S' You can express seconds and days as integers or floats. All other input values must be expressed as integers. For more details, see Details on SQL Standard input . ISO 8601 INTERVAL 'P1Y2M3DT4H5M6S' Traditional PostgreSQL INTERVAL '1 year 2 months 3 days 4 hours 5 minutes 6 seconds' Abbreviated PostgreSQL INTERVAL '1 yr 2 mons 3 d 4 hrs 5 mins 6 secs'

supporting_evidence.section_heading: INTERVAL / ​ Syntax

evidence_span.text: Format Description

supporting_evidence.section_heading: INTERVAL / ​ Syntax

evidence_span.text: SQL Standard INTERVAL 'Y-M D H:M:S' You can express seconds and days as integers or floats. All other input values must be expressed as integers. For more details, see Details on SQL Standard input .

supporting_evidence.section_heading: INTERVAL / ​ Syntax

evidence_span.text: ISO 8601 INTERVAL 'P1Y2M3DT4H5M6S'

supporting_evidence.section_heading: INTERVAL / ​ Syntax

evidence_span.text: Traditional PostgreSQL INTERVAL '1 year 2 months 3 days 4 hours 5 minutes 6 seconds'

supporting_evidence.section_heading: INTERVAL / ​ Syntax

evidence_span.text: Abbreviated PostgreSQL INTERVAL '1 yr 2 mons 3 d 4 hrs 5 mins 6 secs'

supporting_evidence.section_heading: INTERVAL / ​ Syntax

evidence_span.text: By default, CockroachDB displays INTERVAL values in the traditional PostgreSQL format (e.g., INTERVAL '1 year 2 months 3 days 4 hours 5 minutes 6 seconds' ). To change the display format of INTERVAL values, set the intervalstyle or the sql.defaults.intervalstyle to a supported format ( iso_8601 for the ISO 8601 format; sql_standard for the SQL Standard format).

supporting_evidence.section_heading: INTERVAL / ​ Syntax

evidence_span.text: The value of intervalstyle affects how CockroachDB parses certain INTERVAL values. Specifically, when intervalstyle = 'sql_standard' , and when the INTERVAL value begins with a negative symbol, CockroachDB parses all fields as negative values (e.g., -3 years 1 day is parsed as -(3 years 1 day) , or -3 years, -1 day ). When intervalstyle = 'postgres' (the default format), and when the INTERVAL value begins with a negative symbol, CockroachDB only applies the negative symbol to the field that it directly precedes (e.g., -3 years 1 day is parsed as -3 years, +1 day ).

supporting_evidence.section_heading: INTERVAL / ​ Syntax

evidence_span.text: Use instead of the sql.defaults.* . This allows you to set a default value for all users for any that applies during login, making the sql.defaults.* cluster settings redundant.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: INTERVAL / ​ Syntax

evidence_span.text: ​ Details on SQL Standard input

supporting_evidence.section_heading: INTERVAL / ​ Syntax

evidence_span.text: Without a precision or duration field specified, expect the following behavior from SQL Standard input ( Y-M D H:M:S ):

supporting_evidence.section_heading: INTERVAL / ​ Syntax / ​ Details on SQL Standard input

evidence_span.text: Using a single value defines seconds only. For example, INTERVAL '1' is parsed as 00:00:01 .

supporting_evidence.section_heading: INTERVAL / ​ Syntax / ​ Details on SQL Standard input

evidence_span.text: Using two colon-separated integers defines hours and minutes. For example, INTERVAL '1:2' is parsed as 01:02:00 .

supporting_evidence.section_heading: INTERVAL / ​ Syntax / ​ Details on SQL Standard input

evidence_span.text: If the second of two colon-separated values is a float, the interval is parsed as minutes and seconds ( M:S.fff ). For example, INTERVAL '1:2.345' is parsed as 00:01:02.345 .

supporting_evidence.section_heading: INTERVAL / ​ Syntax / ​ Details on SQL Standard input

evidence_span.text: If the first element of the input directly preceding a colon is specified as a float, the interval is parsed as D H:M . For example, INTERVAL '1.2:03:04' is parsed as 1 day 07:52:00 .

supporting_evidence.section_heading: INTERVAL / ​ Syntax / ​ Details on SQL Standard input

evidence_span.text: If the day is omitted, no day value will be stored. For example, INTERVAL '1-2 3:4:5' is parsed as 1 year 2 mons 03:04:05 , and INTERVAL 1-2 is parsed as 1 year 2 mons .

supporting_evidence.section_heading: INTERVAL / ​ Syntax / ​ Details on SQL Standard input

evidence_span.text: If the year and month are omitted, no year or month value will be stored. For example, INTERVAL '1 2:3:4 is parsed as 1 day 02:03:04 .

supporting_evidence.section_heading: INTERVAL / ​ Syntax / ​ Details on SQL Standard input

evidence_span.text: ​ Size

supporting_evidence.section_heading: INTERVAL

evidence_span.text: An INTERVAL column supports values up to 24 bytes in width, but the total storage size is likely to be larger due to CockroachDB metadata. Intervals are stored internally as months, days, and microseconds.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: INTERVAL / ​ Size

evidence_span.text: ​ Precision

supporting_evidence.section_heading: INTERVAL

evidence_span.text: CockroachDB supports precision levels from 0 (seconds) to 6 (microseconds) for INTERVAL values. Precision in time values specifies the number of fractional digits retained in the seconds field. By default, INTERVAL values have a precision of 6 (microseconds).

supporting_evidence.section_heading: INTERVAL / ​ Precision

evidence_span.text: For example, specifying an INTERVAL value as INTERVAL(3) truncates the time precision to milliseconds.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: INTERVAL / ​ Precision

evidence_span.text: ​ Duration fields

supporting_evidence.section_heading: INTERVAL

evidence_span.text: CockroachDB supports duration fields for INTERVAL values. You can specify SECOND , MINUTE , HOUR , or DAY units of duration in the form INTERVAL ... <unit> or INTERVAL ... <unit> TO <unit> .

supporting_evidence.section_heading: INTERVAL / ​ Duration fields

evidence_span.text: Specifying a single duration field truncates the interval at the unit specified, defining the interval as having the duration field unit as its least-significant unit. For example, INTERVAL '1 2:03:04' HOUR truncates the input to an exact hour, and parses the interval as 1 day 02:00:00 .

supporting_evidence.section_heading: INTERVAL / ​ Duration fields

evidence_span.text: A single duration field can also resolve ambiguity in the input. For example, INTERVAL '1' parses the interval as 00:00:01 (1 second). INTERVAL '1' MINUTE parses the interval as 00:01:00 (1 minute).

supporting_evidence.section_heading: INTERVAL / ​ Duration fields

evidence_span.text: If the interval input is ambiguous, specifying two duration fields stores the interval in the units specified. For example, INTERVAL '02:03' MINUTE TO SECOND parses the interval as 00:02:03 (in minutes and seconds). Without MINUTE TO SECOND , the input would be parsed as 02:03:00 (in hours and minutes).

supporting_evidence.section_heading: INTERVAL / ​ Duration fields

evidence_span.text: ​ Example

supporting_evidence.section_heading: INTERVAL

evidence_span.text: > CREATE TABLE intervals (a INT PRIMARY KEY, b INTERVAL);

supporting_evidence.section_heading: INTERVAL / ​ Example

evidence_span.text: > SHOW COLUMNS FROM intervals;

supporting_evidence.section_heading: INTERVAL / ​ Example

evidence_span.text:

--------------+-----------+-------------+----------------+-----------------------+-----------+------------
  a           | INT8      |    false    | NULL           |                       | {primary} |   false
  b           | INTERVAL  |    true     | NULL           |                       | {primary} |   false
(2 rows)

supporting_evidence.section_heading: INTERVAL / ​ Example

evidence_span.text:
> INSERT INTO
    intervals
    VALUES (1, INTERVAL '1 year 2 months 3 days 4 hours 5 minutes 6 seconds'),
           (2, INTERVAL '1-2 3 4:5:6'),
           (3, '1-2 3 4:5:6');

supporting_evidence.section_heading: INTERVAL / ​ Example

evidence_span.text: > SELECT * FROM intervals;

evidence_span.text: ​ Supported casting and conversion

supporting_evidence.section_heading: INTERVAL

evidence_span.text: You can INTERVAL values to any of the following data types:

supporting_evidence.section_heading: INTERVAL / ​ Supported casting and conversion

evidence_span.text: Type Details INT Converts to number of seconds (second precision) DECIMAL Converts to number of seconds (microsecond precision) FLOAT Converts to number of seconds (microsecond precision) STRING Converts to h-m-s format (microsecond precision) TIME Converts to HH:MM:SS.SSSSSS , the time equivalent to the interval after midnight (microsecond precision)

supporting_evidence.section_heading: BIT

evidence_span.text: The BIT and VARBIT stores bit arrays. With BIT , the length is fixed; with VARBIT , the length can be variable.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: BIT

evidence_span.text: ​ Aliases

supporting_evidence.section_heading: BIT

evidence_span.text: The name BIT VARYING is an alias for VARBIT .

supporting_evidence.section_heading: BIT / ​ Aliases

evidence_span.text: ​ Syntax

supporting_evidence.section_heading: BIT

evidence_span.text: Bit array constants are expressed as literals. For example, B'100101' denotes an array of 6 bits.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: BIT / ​ Syntax

evidence_span.text: For more information about bit array constants, see the .

evidence_span.text: ​ Size

supporting_evidence.section_heading: BIT

evidence_span.text: The number of bits in a BIT value is determined as follows:

supporting_evidence.section_heading: BIT / ​ Size

supporting_evidence.section_heading: BIT / ​ Size

evidence_span.text: The effective size of a BIT value is larger than its logical number of bits by a bounded constant factor. Internally, CockroachDB stores bit arrays in increments of 64 bits plus an extra integer value to encode the length.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: BIT / ​ Size

evidence_span.text: The total size of a BIT value can be arbitrarily large, but it is recommended to keep values under 1 MB to ensure performance. Above that threshold, write amplification and other considerations may cause significant performance degradation.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: BIT / ​ Size

evidence_span.text: ​ Supported casting and conversion

supporting_evidence.section_heading: BIT

evidence_span.text: BIT values can be to any of the following data types:

supporting_evidence.section_heading: BIT / ​ Supported casting and conversion

evidence_span.text: Type Details INT Converts the bit array to the corresponding numeric value, interpreting the bits as if the value was encoded using two’s complement . If the bit array is larger than the integer type, excess bits on the left are ignored. For example, B'1010'::INT equals 10 . STRING Prints out the binary digits as a string. This recovers the literal representation. For example, B'1010'::STRING equals '1010' .

evidence_span.text: pg_total_relation_size(relation_oid: oid) -> int Returns the on-disk size, in bytes, of the relation with the given OID, including all indexes and any data still occupying the table’s keyspace (such as dropped-index data awaiting garbage collection). The size is read from a periodically-refreshed cache and may lag behind the true value by minutes. Returns NULL if no such relation exists or has no on-disk representation. Volatile

evidence_span.text: The LTREE stores hierarchical tree-like structures as a label path , which is a sequence of dot-separated labels . Labels represent positions in a tree hierarchy. LTREE is useful for efficiently querying and managing hierarchical data without using recursive joins.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: LTREE

evidence_span.text: The LTREE stores hierarchical tree-like structures as a label path , which is a sequence of dot-separated labels . Labels represent positions in a tree hierarchy. LTREE is useful for efficiently querying and managing hierarchical data without using recursive joins.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: LTREE

evidence_span.text: ​ Syntax

supporting_evidence.section_heading: LTREE

evidence_span.text: Each label in an LTREE label path represents a level in the hierarchy, beginning from the root ( Animals in the following example):

supporting_evidence.section_heading: LTREE / ​ Syntax

evidence_span.text: SELECT 'Animals.Mammals.Carnivora'::LTREE;

supporting_evidence.section_heading: LTREE / ​ Syntax

evidence_span.text:
ltree
-----------------------------
  Animals.Mammals.Carnivora

supporting_evidence.section_heading: LTREE / ​ Syntax

evidence_span.text: Each label in the path must contain only alphanumeric characters ( A - Z , a - z , 0 - 9 ), underscores ( _ ), and hyphens ( - ). The maximum label length is 1,000 characters, and the maximum number of labels in a path is 65,535.

evidence_span.text: The size of an LTREE value is variable and equals the total number of characters in all labels plus the total number of dot separators. Cockroach Labs recommends keeping values below 64 kilobytes. Above that threshold, and other considerations may cause significant performance degradation.

evidence_span.text: The following LTREE comparison and containment operators are valid:

supporting_evidence.section_heading: LTREE / ​ Operators

evidence_span.text: = (equals). Compare paths for equality.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: LTREE / ​ Operators

evidence_span.text: <> , != (not equal to). Compare paths for inequality.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: LTREE / ​ Operators

evidence_span.text: < , <= , > , >= (ordering). Compare paths lexicographically.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: LTREE / ​ Operators

evidence_span.text: @> (is ancestor of). Returns true if the left operand is an ancestor of (or equal to) the right operand.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: LTREE / ​ Operators

evidence_span.text: <@ (is descendant of). Returns true if the left operand is a descendant of (or equal to) the right operand.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: LTREE / ​ Operators

evidence_span.text: || (concatenate). Concatenate two LTREE paths.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: LTREE / ​ Operators

evidence_span.text: For LTREE arrays, the following operators return the first matching element:

supporting_evidence.section_heading: LTREE / ​ Operators

evidence_span.text: ?@> (array contains ancestor). Returns the first array element that is an ancestor of the operand.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: LTREE / ​ Operators

evidence_span.text: ?<@ (array contains descendant). Returns the first array element that is a descendant of the operand.

evidence_span.text: By default, INT is an alias for INT8 , which creates 64-bit signed integers. This differs from the PostgreSQL default for INT , which is 32 bits , and may cause issues for your application if it is not written to handle 64-bit integers, whether due to the language your application is written in, or the ORM/framework it uses to generate SQL (if any).

evidence_span.text: For example, JavaScript language runtimes represent numbers as 64-bit floats, which means that the JS runtime can only represent 53 bits of numeric accuracy and thus has a max safe value of 2 53 , or 9007199254740992. This means that the maximum size of a default INT in CockroachDB is much larger than JavaScript can represent as an integer. Visually, the size difference is as follows:

evidence_span.text: Given the above, if a table contains a column with a default-sized INT value, and you are reading from it or writing to it via JavaScript, you will not be able to read and write values to that column correctly. This issue can pop up in a surprising way if you are using a framework that autogenerates both frontend and backend code (such as twirp ). In such cases, you may find that your backend code can handle 64-bit signed integers, but the generated client/frontend code cannot.

evidence_span.text: ​ Size

supporting_evidence.section_heading: INT

evidence_span.text: The different integer types place different constraints on the range of allowable values, but all integers are stored in the same way regardless of type. Smaller values take up less space than larger ones (based on the numeric value, not the data type).

supporting_evidence.section_heading: INT / ​ Size

evidence_span.text: ​ Considerations for 64-bit signed integers

supporting_evidence.section_heading: INT / ​ Size

evidence_span.text: By default, INT is an alias for INT8 , which creates 64-bit signed integers. This differs from the PostgreSQL default for INT , which is 32 bits , and may cause issues for your application if it is not written to handle 64-bit integers, whether due to the language your application is written in, or the ORM/framework it uses to generate SQL (if any).

supporting_evidence.section_heading: INT / ​ Size / ​ Considerations for 64-bit signed integers

evidence_span.text: For example, JavaScript language runtimes represent numbers as 64-bit floats, which means that the JS runtime can only represent 53 bits of numeric accuracy and thus has a max safe value of 2 53 , or 9007199254740992. This means that the maximum size of a default INT in CockroachDB is much larger than JavaScript can represent as an integer. Visually, the size difference is as follows:

supporting_evidence.section_heading: INT / ​ Size / ​ Considerations for 64-bit signed integers

evidence_span.text:
9223372036854775807 # INT default max value
   9007199254740991 # JS integer max value

supporting_evidence.section_heading: INT / ​ Size / ​ Considerations for 64-bit signed integers

evidence_span.text: Given the above, if a table contains a column with a default-sized INT value, and you are reading from it or writing to it via JavaScript, you will not be able to read and write values to that column correctly. This issue can pop up in a surprising way if you are using a framework that autogenerates both frontend and backend code (such as twirp ). In such cases, you may find that your backend code can handle 64-bit signed integers, but the generated client/frontend code cannot.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: INT / ​ Size / ​ Considerations for 64-bit signed integers

evidence_span.text: st_isvalid(geometry: geometry, flags: int ) -> bool Returns whether the geometry is valid. For flags=0, validity is defined by the OGC spec. evidence_span.text: TIMETZ , which converts TIME values with a specified time zone offset from UTC. Ordering for TIMETZ is done in terms of epoch . Time zones with lesser values are ranked higher if times are equal. For example, '2:00-1' > '2:00+0' and '12:00-1' > '1:00+0' . Like PostgreSQL , we implement the TIMETZ variant for . description.value: TIMETZ , which converts TIME values with a specified time zone offset from UTC. Ordering for TIMETZ is done in terms of epoch . Time zones with lesser values are ranked higher if times are equal. For example, '2:00-1' > '2:00+0' and '12:00-1' > '1:00+0' . Like PostgreSQL , we implement the TIMETZ variant for . We also implement the TIMETZ variant for compatibility with ORMs, like .

evidence_span.text: CockroachDB supports precision levels from 0 (seconds) to 6 (microseconds) for TIME / TIMETZ values. Precision in time values specifies the number of fractional digits retained in the seconds field. For example, specifying a TIME value as TIME(3) truncates the time precision to milliseconds. By default, TIME / TIMETZ values have a precision of 6 (microseconds).

supporting_evidence.section_heading: TIME / TIMETZ

evidence_span.text: The TIME stores the time of day in UTC.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: TIME / TIMETZ

evidence_span.text: The TIMETZ data type stores a time of day with a time zone offset from UTC.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: TIME / TIMETZ

evidence_span.text: ​ Variants

supporting_evidence.section_heading: TIME / TIMETZ

evidence_span.text: TIME has two variants:

supporting_evidence.section_heading: TIME / TIMETZ / ​ Variants

evidence_span.text: TIME , which presents all TIME values in UTC.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: TIME / TIMETZ / ​ Variants

evidence_span.text: TIMETZ , which converts TIME values with a specified time zone offset from UTC. Ordering for TIMETZ is done in terms of epoch . Time zones with lesser values are ranked higher if times are equal. For example, '2:00-1' > '2:00+0' and '12:00-1' > '1:00+0' . Like PostgreSQL , we implement the TIMETZ variant for . We also implement the TIMETZ variant for compatibility with ORMs, like .

supporting_evidence.section_heading: TIME / TIMETZ / ​ Variants

evidence_span.text: You can use the and functions to convert a TIMETZ into a TIME at a specified timezone, or to convert a TIME into a TIMETZ at a specified timezone.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: TIME / TIMETZ / ​ Variants

evidence_span.text: We recommend always using TIME instead of TIMETZ . Convert UTC values to the appropriate time zone on the client side.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: TIME / TIMETZ / ​ Variants

supporting_evidence.section_heading: TIME / TIMETZ

supporting_evidence.section_heading: TIME / TIMETZ / ​ Aliases

evidence_span.text: ​ Syntax

supporting_evidence.section_heading: TIME / TIMETZ

evidence_span.text: ​ TIME

supporting_evidence.section_heading: TIME / TIMETZ / ​ Syntax

evidence_span.text: A constant value of type TIME can be expressed using an , or a string literal type TIME or type TIME . When it is unambiguous, a simple unannotated can also be automatically interpreted as type TIME .

supporting_evidence.section_heading: TIME / TIMETZ / ​ Syntax / ​ TIME

evidence_span.text: The string format for TIME is HH:MM:SS.SSSSSS . For example: TIME '05:40:00.000001' . The fractional portion is optional and is rounded to microseconds (i.e., six digits after the decimal) for compatibility with the PostgreSQL wire protocol .

supporting_evidence.section_heading: TIME / TIMETZ / ​ Syntax / ​ TIME

evidence_span.text: A date of 0000-01-01 is displayed for all TIME / TIMETZ values, but is not stored in the database. To print without a date, you can cast the type to a STRING .

supporting_evidence.section_heading: TIME / TIMETZ / ​ Syntax / ​ TIME

evidence_span.text: A time zone offset of +00:00 is also displayed for all TIME and values, but is not stored in the database.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: TIME / TIMETZ / ​ Syntax / ​ TIME

evidence_span.text: ​ TIMETZ

supporting_evidence.section_heading: TIME / TIMETZ / ​ Syntax

evidence_span.text: To express a TIMETZ value with a time zone offset from UTC, you can add an offset to a TIME value. For example, TIMETZ '10:10:10.555555-05:00' offsets from UTC by -5.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: TIME / TIMETZ / ​ Syntax / ​ TIMETZ

evidence_span.text: If no time zone is specified for a TIMETZ value, the timezone is used. For example, if you for a session using SET TIME ZONE -2 , and you define the TIMETZ as TIMETZ '10:10:10.55' , the value will be displayed with an offset of -2 from UTC.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: TIME / TIMETZ / ​ Syntax / ​ TIMETZ

evidence_span.text: TIMETZ is not affected by session-scoped offsets (unlike ). Time zone offsets only apply to values inserted after the offset has been set, and do not affect existing TIMETZ values, or TIMETZ values with a time zone offset specified.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: TIME / TIMETZ / ​ Syntax / ​ TIMETZ

evidence_span.text: ​ Size

supporting_evidence.section_heading: TIME / TIMETZ

evidence_span.text: A TIME column supports values up to 8 bytes in width, but the total storage size is likely to be larger due to CockroachDB metadata.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: TIME / TIMETZ / ​ Size

evidence_span.text: A TIMETZ column supports values up to 12 bytes in width, but the total storage size is likely to be larger due to CockroachDB metadata.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: TIME / TIMETZ / ​ Size

evidence_span.text: ​ Precision

supporting_evidence.section_heading: TIME / TIMETZ

evidence_span.text: CockroachDB supports precision levels from 0 (seconds) to 6 (microseconds) for TIME / TIMETZ values. Precision in time values specifies the number of fractional digits retained in the seconds field. For example, specifying a TIME value as TIME(3) truncates the time precision to milliseconds. By default, TIME / TIMETZ values have a precision of 6 (microseconds).

supporting_evidence.section_heading: TIME / TIMETZ / ​ Precision

evidence_span.text: You can use an statement to change the precision level of a TIME -typed column. If there is already a non-default precision level specified for the column, the precision level can only be changed to an equal or greater precision level. For an example, see Create a table with a TIME -typed column, with precision .

evidence_span.text: The TSVECTOR stores a list of lexemes, optionally with integer positions and weights. TSVECTOR values are used in .

supporting_evidence.section_heading: TSVECTOR

evidence_span.text: ​ Syntax

supporting_evidence.section_heading: TSVECTOR

evidence_span.text: A TSVECTOR comprises individual lexemes in the form: 'These' 'lexemes' 'are' 'not' 'normalized' 'lexemes.' .

supporting_evidence.section_heading: TSVECTOR / ​ Syntax

evidence_span.text: You can optionally add the following to each lexeme:

supporting_evidence.section_heading: TSVECTOR / ​ Syntax

evidence_span.text: One or more comma-separated integer positions: 'These':1 'lexemes':2 'are':3 'not':4 'normalized':5 'lexemes.':6

supporting_evidence.section_heading: TSVECTOR / ​ Syntax

evidence_span.text: A weight letter ( A , B , C , or D ), in combination with an integer position: 'These':1 'lexemes':2B 'are':3 'not':4 'normalized':5A 'lexemes.':6B If not specified, a lexeme’s weight defaults to D . The lexemes in a TSQUERY and TSVECTOR will only match if they have matching weights. For more information about weights, see the PostgreSQL documentation .

supporting_evidence.section_heading: TSVECTOR / ​ Syntax

evidence_span.text: To be usable in , the lexemes must be normalized . You can do this by using the to_tsvector() to convert a string input to TSVECTOR :

supporting_evidence.section_heading: TSVECTOR / ​ Syntax

evidence_span.text: SELECT to_tsvector('These lexemes are not normalized lexemes.');

supporting_evidence.section_heading: VECTOR

evidence_span.text: The VECTOR data type stores fixed-length arrays of floating-point numbers, which represent data points in multi-dimensional space. Vector search is often used in AI applications such as Large Language Models (LLMs) that rely on vector representations.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: VECTOR

evidence_span.text: For details on valid VECTOR comparison operators, refer to Syntax . For the list of supported VECTOR functions, refer to .

supporting_evidence.section_heading: VECTOR

evidence_span.text: VECTOR functionality is compatible with the pgvector extension for PostgreSQL.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: VECTOR

evidence_span.text: ​ Syntax

supporting_evidence.section_heading: VECTOR

evidence_span.text: A VECTOR value is expressed as an of . The array size corresponds to the number of VECTOR dimensions. For example, the following VECTOR has 3 dimensions:

supporting_evidence.section_heading: VECTOR / ​ Syntax
VECTOR / ​ Syntax

evidence_span.text: You can specify the dimensions when defining a VECTOR column. This will enforce the number of dimensions in the column values. For example:

supporting_evidence.section_heading: VECTOR / ​ Syntax

evidence_span.text: ALTER TABLE foo ADD COLUMN bar VECTOR(3);

supporting_evidence.section_heading: VECTOR / ​ Syntax

evidence_span.text: The following VECTOR comparison operators are valid:

supporting_evidence.section_heading: VECTOR / ​ Syntax

evidence_span.text: = (equals). Compare vectors for equality in filtering and conditional queries.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: VECTOR / ​ Syntax

evidence_span.text: <> (not equal to). Compare vectors for inequality in filtering and conditional queries.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: VECTOR / ​ Syntax

evidence_span.text: <-> (L2 distance). Calculate the Euclidean distance between two vectors, as used in nearest neighbor search and clustering algorithms.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: VECTOR / ​ Syntax

evidence_span.text: <#> (negative inner product). Calculate the inner product of two vectors, as used in similarity searches where the inner product can represent the similarity score.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: VECTOR / ​ Syntax

evidence_span.text: <=> (cosine distance). Calculate the cosine distance between vectors, such as in text and image similarity measures where the orientation of vectors is more important than their magnitude.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: VECTOR / ​ Syntax

supporting_evidence.section_heading: VECTOR

supporting_evidence.section_heading: CITEXT

evidence_span.text: The CITEXT represents a case-insensitive string. Like STRING values, CITEXT values preserve their casing when stored and retrieved. Unlike STRING values, comparisons between CITEXT values are case-insensitive for all Unicode characters that have a defined uppercase/lowercase mapping (e.g., 'É' = 'é' ).

supporting_evidence.section_heading: CITEXT

evidence_span.text: Equality operators ( = , != , <> ) and ordering operators ( < , > , etc.) treat CITEXT values as case-insensitive by default. Refer to the example .

supporting_evidence.section_heading: CITEXT

evidence_span.text: CITEXT compares values as a STRING column with the und-u-ks-level2 , meaning it is case-insensitive but accent-sensitive.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: CITEXT

supporting_evidence.section_heading: CITEXT

evidence_span.text: As with STRING , CITEXT values should be kept below 64 KB for best performance. Because CITEXT values resort to a collation engine on every comparison, CITEXT columns and indexes consume marginally more CPU and memory than their STRING equivalents.

evidence_span.text: To declare a new enumerated data type, use :

supporting_evidence.section_heading: ENUM / ​ Syntax

evidence_span.text: > CREATE TYPE <name> AS ENUM ('<value1', '<value2', ...);

supporting_evidence.section_heading: ENUM / ​ Syntax

evidence_span.text: where <name is the name of the new type, and <value1, <value2>, ... are string literals that make up the type’s set of static values.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: ENUM / ​ Syntax

evidence_span.text: You can qualify the <name of an enumerated type with a (e.g., db.typename ). After the type is created, it can only be referenced from the database that contains the type.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: ENUM / ​ Syntax

evidence_span.text: To show all ENUM types in the database, including all ENUMS created implicitly for , use :

supporting_evidence.section_heading: ENUM / ​ Syntax

evidence_span.text: > SHOW ENUMS;

supporting_evidence.section_heading: ENUM / ​ Syntax

evidence_span.text: To modify an ENUM type, use :

supporting_evidence.section_heading: ENUM / ​ Syntax

evidence_span.text: > ALTER TYPE <name> ADD VALUE '<value';

supporting_evidence.section_heading: ENUM / ​ Syntax

evidence_span.text: where <value is a string literal to add to the existing list of type values. You can also use ALTER TYPE to rename types, rename type values, set a type’s schema, or change the type owner’s .

supporting_evidence.section_heading: ENUM / ​ Syntax

evidence_span.text: To drop the type, use :

supporting_evidence.section_heading: ENUM / ​ Syntax

evidence_span.text: > DROP TYPE <name>;

evidence_span.text: To express a byte array constant, see the section on for more details. For example, the following three are equivalent literals for the same byte array: b'abc' , b'\141\142\143' , b'\x61\x62\x63' .

evidence_span.text: ​ Size

supporting_evidence.section_heading: BYTES

evidence_span.text: The size of a BYTES value is variable, but it’s recommended to keep values under 1 MB to ensure adequate performance. Above that threshold, and other considerations may cause significant performance degradation.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: BYTES / ​ Size

evidence_span.text: We strongly recommend adding size limits to all , which includes columns in .

supporting_evidence.section_heading: BYTES / ​ Size

evidence_span.text: Values exceeding 1 MiB can lead to and cause significant performance degradation or even .

evidence_span.text: ​ Supported conversions

supporting_evidence.section_heading: BYTES

evidence_span.text: BYTES values can be explicitly to . This conversion always succeeds. Two conversion modes are supported, controlled by the bytea_output :

supporting_evidence.section_heading: BYTES / ​ Supported conversions

evidence_span.text: hex (default): The output of the conversion starts with the two characters \ , x and the rest of the string is composed by the hexadecimal encoding of each byte in the input. For example, x'48AA'::STRING produces '\x48AA' .

supporting_evidence.section_heading: BYTES / ​ Supported conversions

evidence_span.text: escape : The output of the conversion contains each byte in the input, as-is if it is an ASCII character, or encoded using the octal escape format \NNN otherwise. For example, x'48AA'::STRING produces '0\252' .

supporting_evidence.section_heading: BYTES / ​ Supported conversions

evidence_span.text: STRING values can be cast explicitly to BYTES . This conversion will fail if the hexadecimal digits are not valid, or if there is an odd number of them. Two conversion modes are supported:

supporting_evidence.section_heading: BYTES / ​ Supported conversions

evidence_span.text: If the string starts with the two special characters \ and x (e.g., \xAABB ), the rest of the string is interpreted as a sequence of hexadecimal digits. The string is then converted to a byte array where each pair of hexadecimal digits is converted to one byte.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: BYTES / ​ Supported conversions

evidence_span.text: Otherwise, the string is converted to a byte array that contains its UTF-8 encoding.

evidence_span.text: CockroachDB supports precision levels from 0 (seconds) to 6 (microseconds) for TIMESTAMP / TIMESTAMPTZ values. Precision in time values specifies the number of fractional digits retained in the seconds field. For example, specifying a TIMESTAMPTZ value as TIMESTAMPTZ(3) truncates the time component to milliseconds. By default, TIMESTAMP / TIMESTAMPTZ values have a precision of 6 (microseconds).

evidence_span.text: CockroachDB does not support an infinity / -infinity representation for TIMESTAMP casts. Instead, infinity::TIMESTAMP evaluates to 294276-12-31 23:59:59.999999+00:00 , the maximum TIMESTAMP value supported, and -infinity::TIMESTAMP evaluates to -4714-11-24 00:00:00+00:00 , the minimum TIMESTAMP value supported.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: TIMESTAMP / TIMESTAMPTZ

evidence_span.text: The TIMESTAMP and TIMESTAMPTZ store a date and time pair in UTC.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: TIMESTAMP / TIMESTAMPTZ

evidence_span.text: ​ Variants

supporting_evidence.section_heading: TIMESTAMP / TIMESTAMPTZ

evidence_span.text: TIMESTAMP has two variants:

supporting_evidence.section_heading: TIMESTAMP / TIMESTAMPTZ / ​ Variants

evidence_span.text: TIMESTAMP presents all TIMESTAMP values in UTC.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: TIMESTAMP / TIMESTAMPTZ / ​ Variants

evidence_span.text: TIMESTAMPTZ converts TIMESTAMP values from UTC to the client’s session time zone (unless another time zone is specified for the value). However, it is conceptually important to note that TIMESTAMPTZ does not store any time zone data.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: TIMESTAMP / TIMESTAMPTZ / ​ Variants

evidence_span.text: The default session time zone is UTC, which means that by default TIMESTAMPTZ values display in UTC.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: TIMESTAMP / TIMESTAMPTZ / ​ Variants

evidence_span.text: The difference between these two variants is that TIMESTAMPTZ uses the client’s session , while the other simply does not. This behavior extends to functions like now() and extract() on TIMESTAMPTZ values.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: TIMESTAMP / TIMESTAMPTZ / ​ Variants

evidence_span.text: A time zone offset of +00:00 is displayed for all and TIMESTAMP values, but is not stored in the database.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: TIMESTAMP / TIMESTAMPTZ / ​ Variants

evidence_span.text: You can use the and functions to convert a TIMESTAMPTZ into a TIMESTAMP at a specified timezone, or to convert a TIMESTAMP into a TIMESTAMPTZ at a specified timezone.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: TIMESTAMP / TIMESTAMPTZ / ​ Variants

evidence_span.text: Explore the differences of TIMESTAMP and TIMESTAMPTZ in the following video:

supporting_evidence.section_heading: TIMESTAMP / TIMESTAMPTZ / ​ Variants

evidence_span.text: ​ Best practices

supporting_evidence.section_heading: TIMESTAMP / TIMESTAMPTZ

evidence_span.text: We recommend always using the TIMESTAMPTZ variant because the TIMESTAMP variant can sometimes lead to unexpected behaviors when it ignores a session offset. However, we also recommend you avoid for your database.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: TIMESTAMP / TIMESTAMPTZ / ​ Best practices

evidence_span.text: ​ Aliases

supporting_evidence.section_heading: TIMESTAMP / TIMESTAMPTZ

evidence_span.text: In CockroachDB, the following are aliases:

supporting_evidence.section_heading: TIMESTAMP / TIMESTAMPTZ / ​ Aliases

evidence_span.text: TIMESTAMP , TIMESTAMP WITHOUT TIME ZONE

supporting_evidence.section_heading: TIMESTAMP / TIMESTAMPTZ / ​ Aliases

evidence_span.text: TIMESTAMPTZ , TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE

supporting_evidence.section_heading: TIMESTAMP / TIMESTAMPTZ / ​ Aliases

evidence_span.text: ​ Syntax

supporting_evidence.section_heading: TIMESTAMP / TIMESTAMPTZ

evidence_span.text: You can express a constant value of type TIMESTAMP / TIMESTAMPTZ using an , or a string literal type TIMESTAMP / TIMESTAMPTZ or type TIMESTAMP / TIMESTAMPTZ . When it is unambiguous, a simple unannotated is automatically interpreted as type TIMESTAMP or TIMESTAMPTZ .

supporting_evidence.section_heading: TIMESTAMP / TIMESTAMPTZ / ​ Syntax

evidence_span.text: You can express TIMESTAMP constants using the following string literal formats:

supporting_evidence.section_heading: TIMESTAMP / TIMESTAMPTZ / ​ Syntax

evidence_span.text: Format Example Date only TIMESTAMP '2016-01-25' Date and Time TIMESTAMP '2016-01-25 10:10:10.555555' ISO 8601 TIMESTAMP '2016-01-25T10:10:10.555555'

supporting_evidence.section_heading: TIMESTAMP / TIMESTAMPTZ / ​ Syntax

evidence_span.text: Format Example

supporting_evidence.section_heading: TIMESTAMP / TIMESTAMPTZ / ​ Syntax

evidence_span.text: Date only TIMESTAMP '2016-01-25'

supporting_evidence.section_heading: TIMESTAMP / TIMESTAMPTZ / ​ Syntax

evidence_span.text: Date and Time TIMESTAMP '2016-01-25 10:10:10.555555'

supporting_evidence.section_heading: TIMESTAMP / TIMESTAMPTZ / ​ Syntax
TIMESTAMP / TIMESTAMPTZ / ​ Syntax

evidence_span.text: To express a TIMESTAMPTZ value with time zone offset from UTC, use the following format: TIMESTAMPTZ '2016-01-25 10:10:10.555555-05:00' . The fractional portion is optional and is rounded to microseconds (6 digits after decimal) for compatibility with the PostgreSQL wire protocol.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: TIMESTAMP / TIMESTAMPTZ / ​ Syntax

evidence_span.text: By default, CockroachDB interprets truncated dates (e.g., 12-16-06 ) as MM-DD-YY . To change the input string format of truncated dates, set the datestyle or the sql.defaults.datestyle .

supporting_evidence.section_heading: TIMESTAMP / TIMESTAMPTZ / ​ Syntax

evidence_span.text: Use instead of the sql.defaults.* . This allows you to set a default value for all users for any that applies during login, making the sql.defaults.* cluster settings redundant.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: TIMESTAMP / TIMESTAMPTZ / ​ Syntax

evidence_span.text: ​ Size

supporting_evidence.section_heading: TIMESTAMP / TIMESTAMPTZ

evidence_span.text: A TIMESTAMP / TIMESTAMPTZ column supports values up to 12 bytes in width, but the total storage size is likely to be larger due to CockroachDB metadata.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: TIMESTAMP / TIMESTAMPTZ / ​ Size

evidence_span.text: ​ Precision

supporting_evidence.section_heading: TIMESTAMP / TIMESTAMPTZ

evidence_span.text: CockroachDB supports precision levels from 0 (seconds) to 6 (microseconds) for TIMESTAMP / TIMESTAMPTZ values. Precision in time values specifies the number of fractional digits retained in the seconds field. For example, specifying a TIMESTAMPTZ value as TIMESTAMPTZ(3) truncates the time component to milliseconds. By default, TIMESTAMP / TIMESTAMPTZ values have a precision of 6 (microseconds).

supporting_evidence.section_heading: TIMESTAMP / TIMESTAMPTZ / ​ Precision

evidence_span.text: You can use an statement to change the precision level of a TIMESTAMP / TIMESTAMPTZ -typed column. If there is already a non-default precision level specified for the column, the precision level can only be changed to an equal or greater precision level. For an example, see Create a table with a TIMESTAMP -typed column, with precision .

supporting_evidence.section_heading: TIMESTAMP / TIMESTAMPTZ / ​ Precision

evidence_span.text: ​ Supported casting and conversion

supporting_evidence.section_heading: TIMESTAMP / TIMESTAMPTZ

evidence_span.text: TIMESTAMP values can be to any of the following data types:

supporting_evidence.section_heading: TIMESTAMP / TIMESTAMPTZ / ​ Supported casting and conversion

evidence_span.text: Type Details DECIMAL Converts to number of seconds since the Unix epoch (Jan. 1, 1970). FLOAT Converts to number of seconds since the Unix epoch (Jan. 1, 1970). TIME Converts to the time portion ( HH:MM:SS ) of the timestamp. INT Converts to number of seconds since the Unix epoch (Jan. 1, 1970). DATE Converts to the date ( YYYY-MM-DD ) of the timestamp and omits the other information. STRING Converts to the date and time portion ( YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS ) of the timestamp and omits the time zone offset.

evidence_span.text: ​ Infinity TIMESTAMP casts

supporting_evidence.section_heading: TIMESTAMP / TIMESTAMPTZ / ​ Supported casting and conversion

evidence_span.text: CockroachDB does not support an infinity / -infinity representation for TIMESTAMP casts. Instead, infinity::TIMESTAMP evaluates to 294276-12-31 23:59:59.999999+00:00 , the maximum TIMESTAMP value supported, and -infinity::TIMESTAMP evaluates to -4714-11-24 00:00:00+00:00 , the minimum TIMESTAMP value supported.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: TIMESTAMP / TIMESTAMPTZ / ​ Supported casting and conversion / ​ Infinity TIMESTAMP casts

evidence_span.text: Note that this behavior differs from PostgreSQL, for which infinity is higher than any allowable TIMESTAMP value (including 294276-12-31 23:59:59.999999+00:00 ), and -infinity is lower than any allowable TIMESTAMP value (including -4714-11-24 00:00:00+00:00 ).

The value is a combination of the insert timestamp (bit-reversed) and the ID of the node executing the statement, which guarantees this combination is globally unique. When operating on a spheroid, this function will use the sphere to calculate the closest two points. The spheroid distance between these two points is calculated using GeographicLib. This follows observed PostGIS behavior. This function utilizes the S2 library for spherical calculations. This function utilizes the GeographicLib library for spheroid calculations. Immutable
